questions.response:
The **Belgic Confession** (1561), one of the Three Forms of Unity in the Reformed tradition, provides a clear and robust teaching on the **doctrine of original sin** in **Article 15**. Here is a summary of its key points:

### **1. The Universality of Sin (Total Depravity)**
The Confession affirms that **all humans, except Christ, are born with original sin**, which is not merely a weakness but a **corruption of the whole nature** inherited from Adam. This sin is not just an external influence but a **deep-seated corruption** that affects every part of human nature—**mind, will, affections, and body** (cf. Rom. 5:12; Ps. 51:5; Eph. 2:1-3).

> *"We believe that, through the disobedience of Adam, original sin is extended to all mankind; which is a corruption of the whole nature, and an hereditary disease, wherewith infants themselves are infected even in their mother’s womb, and which produceth in man all sorts of sin, being in him as a root thereof, and therefore is so vile and abominable in the sight of God that it is sufficient to condemn all mankind."*

### **2. Inherited Guilt and Corruption**
Original sin is not just a **tendency toward sin** but a **legal guilt** imputed to all humanity because of Adam’s transgression (Rom. 5:18-19). This means:
- **All are born under God’s wrath** (Eph. 2:3).
- **All are incapable of true righteousness** (Rom. 3:10-12).
- **All are subject to death** (Rom. 6:23).

### **3. The Necessity of Christ’s Redemption**
Because of original sin, **no one can be saved by their own works** (Rom. 3:20). Only through **Christ’s atoning work** can sinners be justified and regenerated (Eph. 2:4-9; Titus 3:5).

### **4. The Remnant of Sin in Believers**
Even after regeneration, **sin remains in believers** (Rom. 7:14-25), though it no longer reigns over them (Rom. 6:14). The Confession does not teach **sinless perfection** in this life but affirms the **ongoing struggle against sin** (1 John 1:8-10).

### **Comparison with Other Reformed Confessions**
- The **Heidelberg Catechism** (Q&A 7-8) similarly teaches that humans are **wholly incapable of doing any good** and **inclined to all evil** apart from Christ.
- The **Westminster Confession of Faith** (6.2-3) also affirms **total depravity** and the **imputation of Adam’s sin** to all humanity.

### **Conclusion**
The Belgic Confession presents original sin as:
✔ **Universal** – Affecting all descendants of Adam.
✔ **Total** – Corrupting every part of human nature.
✔ **Inherited** – Passed down from generation to generation.
✔ **Condemning** – Making all deserving of God’s wrath.
✔ **Overcome only by Christ** – Requiring divine grace for salvation.

This doctrine underscores the **necessity of grace** and the **sufficiency of Christ’s work** for salvation. Would you like further clarification on any aspect?

questions.question: What does the Belgic Confession teach about the doctrine of election?
questions.reference_answer: We believe that- all Adam's descendants having thus fallen into perdition and ruin by the sin of Adam- God showed himself to be as he is: merciful and just. God is merciful in withdrawing and saving from this perdition those who, in the eternal and unchangeable divine counsel, have been elected and chosen in Jesus Christ our Lord by his pure goodness, without any consideration of their works. God is just in leaving the others in their ruin and fall into which they plunged themselves.

scoring.rubric: Must address the key points of Article 16 (The Doctrine of Election). Should align with the Belgic Confession's teaching on this topic.

questions.response:
The **Belgic Confession** (1561), written by **Guido de Brès**, is one of the **Three Forms of Unity** in the Reformed tradition, alongside the **Heidelberg Catechism** and the **Canons of Dort**. It presents a clear and biblical doctrine of **election** (or predestination) that aligns with classical Reformed theology. Here are the key teachings on election from the Belgic Confession:

---

### **1. Election is God’s Sovereign Choice (Article 16)**
The Belgic Confession teaches that **election is an unconditional, sovereign act of God** in which He chooses certain individuals for salvation **not based on any foreseen merit or faith** in them, but purely out of His **good pleasure and grace**.

> *"We believe that—all the posterity of Adam being thus fallen into perdition and ruin by the sin of the first man—God did manifest Himself such as He is; that is to say, merciful and just: merciful, since He delivers and preserves from this perdition all whom He, in His eternal and unchangeable counsel, of mere goodness has elected in Christ Jesus our Lord, without any respect to their works; just, in leaving others in the fall and perdition wherein they have involved themselves."* (Article 16)

Key points:
- Election is **not based on human works or foreseen faith** (contra Arminianism).
- It is **rooted in God’s eternal and unchangeable counsel** (His decree).
- It is an act of **pure grace** ("of mere goodness").
- God is **just** in passing over others (reprobation), since all deserve condemnation.

---

### **2. Election is in Christ (Article 16 & 22)**
The Confession emphasizes that election is **centered in Christ**—God chooses His people **in Christ** before the foundation of the world (Eph. 1:4).

> *"We believe that, all the posterity of Adam having thus fallen into perdition and ruin by the sin of the first man, God did manifest Himself such as He is; that is to say, merciful and just: merciful, since He delivers and preserves from this perdition all whom He, in His eternal and unchangeable counsel, of mere goodness has **elected in Christ Jesus our Lord**..."* (Article 16)

> *"We believe that this good pleasure of God is the sole cause of our salvation, and that the faith which He imparts to us is the means whereby we are ingrafted into Christ, who is the only foundation of our salvation."* (Article 22)

Key points:
- Election is **Christocentric**—God’s choice is **in Christ**, not apart from Him.
- Faith is the **means** by which the elect are united to Christ, but it is **not the cause** of election.

---

### **3. Election is Particular (Not Universal) (Article 16)**
The Belgic Confession teaches **particular election**—God does not elect all people, but only a **definite number** (the "elect").

> *"...delivers and preserves from this perdition **all whom He... has elected** in Christ Jesus our Lord, without any respect to their works; just, in leaving others in the fall and perdition wherein they have involved themselves."* (Article 16)

This aligns with the **Canons of Dort** (1619), which later clarified that election is **not based on foreseen faith** (contra Arminianism) and that **not all are elect**.

---

### **4. Election Leads to Perseverance in Faith (Article 27 & 37)**
The Confession teaches that the elect **cannot finally fall away**—God preserves them in faith until the end.

> *"We believe that this holy congregation is an assembly of those who are saved, and that outside of it there is no salvation... We believe that since this holy assembly and congregation is the gathering of those who are saved and there is no salvation apart from it, no one ought to withdraw from it, content to be by himself, regardless of his status or condition. But all people are obliged to join and unite with it, keeping the unity of the church by submitting to its instruction and discipline, by bending their necks under the yoke of Jesus Christ, and by serving to build up one another, according to the gifts God has given them as members of each other in the same body."* (Article 28)

> *"Finally, we believe, according to the Word of God, when the time appointed by the Lord (which is unknown to all creatures) is come, and the number of the elect complete, that our Lord Jesus Christ will come from heaven, corporally and visibly, as He ascended, with great glory and majesty, to declare Himself Judge of the quick and the dead..."* (Article 37)

Key points:
- The elect **persevere in faith** because God preserves them.
- The **number of the elect is complete** (God knows who they are).
- The elect will **certainly be saved** (no possibility of final apostasy).

---

### **5. Reprobation is God’s Just Decree (Article 16)**
The Belgic Confession does not shy away from the **doctrine of reprobation**—God’s sovereign decision to pass over some, leaving them in their sin.

> *"...just, in leaving others in the fall and perdition wherein they have involved themselves."* (Article 16)

This is not an arbitrary act of cruelty but a **just response** to human sin. All deserve condemnation, and God is **not obligated to save anyone**. His mercy in election is **gracious**, while His justice in reprobation is **righteous**.

---

### **6. Election is for God’s Glory (Article 13 & 16)**
The Confession teaches that election **magnifies God’s grace and glory**, not human merit.

> *"We believe that this good pleasure, decree, and counsel of the will of God is the cause of our salvation, and that to God alone belongs the glory of our salvation, without any merit of ours."* (Article 13)

> *"...of mere goodness has elected in Christ Jesus our Lord, **without any respect to their works**."* (Article 16)

Key point:
- Election **exalts God’s grace**, not human free will.

---

### **Comparison with Other Reformed Standards**
- **Heidelberg Catechism (Q&A 54):** Teaches that the elect are gathered into the church by the Holy Spirit.
- **Canons of Dort (1619):** Expands on election, rejecting Arminianism and affirming **unconditional election, limited atonement, irresistible grace, and perseverance of the saints (TULIP)**.
- **Westminster Confession (1646):** Also teaches **unconditional election** and **reprobation**.

The Belgic Confession’s teaching on election is **consistent with these other Reformed standards**, emphasizing **God’s sovereignty, grace, and justice** in salvation.

---

### **Summary of the Belgic Confession’s Teaching on Election**
1. **Unconditional** – Not based on foreseen faith or works.
2. **Sovereign** – God’s free choice, not dependent on man.
3. **In Christ** – The elect are chosen in Him.
4. **Particular** – Not all are elect; God passes over some (reprobation).
5. **Effectual** – The elect will certainly be saved.
6. **For God’s Glory** – Salvation is entirely of grace, not merit.

This doctrine is meant to **humble the sinner, exalt God’s grace, and assure believers of their security in Christ**. It is a **comforting truth** for those who trust in Christ, knowing that their salvation depends **not on their own strength, but on God’s unchanging decree**.

questions.question: What does the Belgic Confession teach about the righteousness of faith?
questions.reference_answer: We believe that for us to acquire the true knowledge of this great mystery the Holy Spirit kindles in our hearts a true faith that embraces Jesus Christ, with all his merits, and makes him its own, and no longer looks for anything apart from him. For it must necessarily follow that either all that is required for our salvation is not in Christ or, if all is in him, then those who have Christ by faith have his salvation entirely. Therefore, to say that Christ is not enough but that something else is needed as well is a most enormous blasphemy against God- for it then would follow that Jesus Christ is only half a Savior. And therefore we justly say with Paul that we are justified "by faith alone" or "by faith apart from works." (Rom. 3:28) However, we do not mean, properly speaking, that it is faith itself that justifies us- for faith is only the instrument by which we embrace Christ, our righteousness. But Jesus Christ is our righteousness in making available to us all his merits and all the holy works he has done for us and in our place. And faith is the instrument that keeps us in communion with him and with all his benefits. When those benefits are made ours, they are more than enough to absolve us of our sins.

scoring.rubric: Must address the key points of Article 22 (The Righteousness of Faith). Should align with the Belgic Confession's teaching on this topic.

questions.response:
The **Belgic Confession** (1561), one of the Three Forms of Unity in the Reformed tradition, teaches a clear and robust doctrine of **justification by faith alone** (*sola fide*), emphasizing that salvation is received through faith in Christ apart from human works. Here are the key points it makes about the **righteousness of faith**:

### **1. Justification by Faith Alone (Article 22)**
The Belgic Confession states that **faith is the sole instrument by which we receive Christ’s righteousness**:
> *"We believe that for us to acquire the true knowledge of this great mystery the Holy Spirit kindles in our hearts a true faith that embraces Jesus Christ, with all his merits, and makes him its own, and no longer looks for anything apart from him. For it must necessarily follow that either all that is required for our salvation is not in Christ or, if all is in him, then he who has Christ by faith has his salvation entirely. Therefore, to say that Christ is not enough but that something else is needed as well is a most enormous blasphemy against God—for it then would follow that Jesus Christ is only half a Savior."*

This means:
- **Faith is not a work** but the **empty hand** that receives Christ’s righteousness.
- **Justification is by faith alone**, not by faith *and* works.
- **Christ’s righteousness is imputed** (credited) to the believer, not infused (as in Roman Catholic theology).

### **2. Faith as the Instrument, Not the Ground, of Justification (Article 23)**
The Confession distinguishes between **faith as the means** and **Christ’s righteousness as the ground** of justification:
> *"We believe that our blessedness lies in the forgiveness of our sins because of Jesus Christ, and that in it our righteousness before God is contained, as David and Paul teach us when they declare that man blessed to whom God grants righteousness apart from works. And the same apostle says that we are justified freely by his grace, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus. And therefore we always hold to this firm foundation, having attached the whole glory to God, humbling ourselves and acknowledging ourselves as we are, not claiming a thing for ourselves or our merits and leaning and resting only on the obedience of Christ crucified, which is ours when we believe in him."*

Key points:
- **Faith is not the righteousness itself** but the **instrument** by which we receive Christ’s righteousness.
- **Justification is by grace alone** (*sola gratia*), not based on human merit.
- **Christ’s obedience (active and passive) is the sole ground** of our acceptance before God.

### **3. Rejection of Works-Righteousness (Article 24)**
The Belgic Confession **explicitly rejects** the idea that good works contribute to justification:
> *"We believe that this true faith, worked in man by the hearing of God’s Word and by the operation of the Holy Spirit, regenerates him and makes him a new man, causing him to live a new life and freeing him from the slavery of sin. Therefore it is so far from being true that this justifying faith makes men remiss in a pious and holy life, that on the contrary without it they would never do anything out of love to God, but only out of self-love or fear of damnation. Therefore it is impossible that this holy faith can be unfruitful in man; for we do not speak of a vain faith, but of such a faith which is called in Scripture a faith working through love, which excites man to the practice of those works which God has commanded in his Word."*

Key distinctions:
- **Good works are the fruit of faith**, not the cause of justification.
- **Faith alone justifies**, but **true faith is never alone**—it always produces good works.
- **Works are evidence of salvation**, not the basis for it.

### **4. Christ’s Righteousness as Our Only Hope (Article 22-23)**
The Confession emphasizes that **Christ’s righteousness is perfect and complete**, leaving no room for human contribution:
> *"For it must necessarily follow that either all that is required for our salvation is not in Christ or, if all is in him, then he who has Christ by faith has his salvation entirely. Therefore, to say that Christ is not enough but that something else is needed as well is a most enormous blasphemy against God—for it then would follow that Jesus Christ is only half a Savior."*

### **Summary of the Belgic Confession’s Teaching on the Righteousness of Faith:**
1. **Justification is by faith alone** (*sola fide*)—not by works, not by faith *and* works.
2. **Faith is the instrument**, not the ground, of justification—Christ’s righteousness is the ground.
3. **Christ’s righteousness is imputed** (credited) to the believer, not infused.
4. **Good works are the fruit of faith**, not the cause of justification.
5. **Justification is by grace alone** (*sola gratia*), apart from human merit.

This aligns with the broader **Reformed doctrine of justification**, as later systematized in the **Westminster Confession of Faith** and the **Heidelberg Catechism**. The Belgic Confession’s teaching remains foundational for Reformed churches today.

questions.question: What does the Belgic Confession teach about the last judgement?
questions.reference_answer: Finally we believe, according to God's Word, that when the time appointed by the Lord is come (which is unknown to all creatures) and the number of the elect is complete, our Lord Jesus Christ will come from heaven, bodily and visibly, as he ascended, with great glory and majesty, to declare himself the judge of the living and the dead. He will burn this old world, in fire and flame, in order to cleanse it. Then all human creatures will appear in person before the great judge- men, women, and children, who have lived from the beginning until the end of the world. They will be summoned there "with the archangel's call and with the sound of God's trumpet." (1 Thess. 4:16) For all those who died before that time will be raised from the earth, their spirits being joined and united with their own bodies in which they lived. And as for those who are still alive, they will not die like the others but will be changed "in the twinkling of an eye" from perishable to imperishable. (1 Cor. 15:51-53) Then the books (that is, the consciences) will be opened, and the dead will be judged according to the things they did in the world, (Rev. 20:12) whether good or evil. Indeed, all people will give account of all the idle words they have spoken, (Matt. 12:36) which the world regards as only playing games. And then the secrets and hypocrisies of all people will be publicly uncovered in the sight of all. Therefore, with good reason the thought of this judgment is horrible and dreadful to wicked and evil people. But it is very pleasant and a great comfort to the righteous and elect, since their total redemption will then be accomplished. They will then receive the fruits of their labor and of the trouble they have suffered; their innocence will be openly recognized by all; and they will see the terrible vengeance that God will bring on the evil ones who tyrannized, oppressed, and tormented them in this world. The evil ones will be convicted by the witness of their own consciences, and shall be made immortal- but only to be tormented in "the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels." (Matt. 25:41) In contrast, the faithful and elect will be crowned with glory and honor. The Son of God will profess their names (Matt. 10:32) before God his Father and the holy and elect angels; all tears will be wiped from their eyes; (Rev. 7:17) and their cause- at present condemned as heretical and evil by many judges and civil officers- will be acknowledged as the cause of the Son of God. And as a gracious reward the Lord will make them possess a glory such as the human heart could never imagine. So we look forward to that great day with longing in order to enjoy fully the promises of God in Christ Jesus, our Lord.

questions.response:
The **Belgic Confession** (1561), one of the Three Forms of Unity in the Reformed tradition, provides a clear and biblical teaching on the **Last Judgment** in **Article 37**. Here is a summary of its key points:

### **1. The Reality of the Last Judgment**
The Confession affirms that there will be a **final, universal judgment** at the end of time, when Christ returns in glory. This judgment is certain and will be executed by **Jesus Christ Himself**, who was ordained by God to be the Judge of the living and the dead (Acts 10:42; 2 Tim. 4:1).

### **2. The Judge: Jesus Christ**
- Christ, who was once judged unjustly by men, will return as the **righteous Judge** (John 5:22, 27).
- He will judge **all people**—both the living and the dead—without partiality (Rom. 2:11; 1 Pet. 4:5).

### **3. The Resurrection of the Dead**
- Before the judgment, the **dead will be raised** (John 5:28-29; 1 Cor. 15:52).

- The present heavens and earth will be **consumed by fire** (2 Pet. 3:10-12).

### **6. The Purpose of the Judgment**
- To **glorify God’s justice** (Rom. 2:5-6).
- To **vindicate the righteous** (1 Thess. 4:16-17).
- To **execute perfect justice** on the wicked (Rev. 20:11-15).

### **7. The Assurance for Believers**
- Believers need not fear the judgment because **Christ has already borne their condemnation** (Rom. 8:1, 33-34).
- They will receive **eternal life** in the presence of God (Rev. 21:3-4).

### **Key Scripture References in Article 37:**
- **Matthew 25:31-46** (Sheep and goats)
- **John 5:22, 27** (Christ as Judge)
- **Acts 17:31** (God has appointed a day of judgment)
- **2 Corinthians 5:10** (All must appear before the judgment seat of Christ)
- **Revelation 20:11-15** (The great white throne judgment)

### **Conclusion**
The Belgic Confession teaches that the **Last Judgment** is a **certain, universal, and final** event where Christ will judge all people according to their deeds. It emphasizes **God’s justice, the resurrection of the dead, and the eternal destinies of the righteous and the wicked**. For believers, this judgment is not a cause for fear but a source of **hope and assurance** in Christ’s finished work.

questions.response:
Article 7 of the **Canons of Dort** (part of the **First Main Point of Doctrine: Divine Election and Rejection**) presents the Reformed doctrine of **unconditional election** in a clear and systematic way. Here is the key teaching from **Article 7**:

> **"Election is the unchangeable purpose of God, whereby, before the foundation of the world, He has out of mere grace, according to the sovereign good pleasure of His own will, chosen from the whole human race, which had fallen through their own fault from their primitive state of rectitude into sin and destruction, a certain number of persons to redemption in Christ, whom He from eternity appointed the Mediator and Head of the elect and the foundation of salvation."**

### **Key Points from Article 7:**
1. **Election is God’s Unchangeable Purpose**
   - God’s choice of the elect is not based on any foreseen merit, faith, or works in them but is an eternal, unchanging decree.

2. **Before the Foundation of the World**
   - Election is not a reaction to human sin but was determined in eternity past, demonstrating God’s sovereignty.

3. **Out of Mere Grace (Sola Gratia)**
   - Election is entirely a gift of God’s grace, not earned or deserved by any human effort.

4. **According to the Sovereign Good Pleasure of His Will**
   - God’s choice is based solely on His own will, not on any condition in the elect (e.g., foreseen faith).

5. **From the Whole Fallen Human Race**
   - Election is not universal but particular—God chooses some out of the mass of fallen humanity.

6. **To Redemption in Christ**
   - The elect are chosen **in Christ**, meaning their salvation is secured through His atoning work.

7. **Christ as the Mediator and Head of the Elect**
   - Christ is the foundation of election; the elect are united to Him by faith, which is itself a gift of God (Eph. 1:4-5; 2:8-9).

### **Contrast with Rejection (Article 15)**
While Article 7 focuses on **election**, the Canons also teach **reprobation** (the passing over of some in God’s decree). However, the Canons emphasize that reprobation is not the same as election—God actively chooses the elect in grace, while the non-elect are left in their just condemnation due to their own sin.

### **Biblical Support**
The Canons root this doctrine in passages such as:
- **Ephesians 1:4-5** – "He chose us in Him before the foundation of the world…"
- **Romans 9:11-16** – "So then it depends not on human will or exertion, but on God, who has mercy."
- **John 15:16** – "You did not choose me, but I chose you…"

### **Conclusion**
Article 7 of the Canons of Dort teaches that **election is unconditional, gracious, and sovereign**, grounded in God’s eternal decree and centered in Christ. It rejects any notion that election is based on human merit or foreseen faith, affirming instead that salvation is entirely of the Lord.

In **Article 9** of the **Canons of Dort** (part of the **First Main Point of Doctrine: Divine Election and Rejection**), the Reformed churches clarify their teaching on **divine predestination**, particularly addressing objections and misconceptions. Here is the key content of Article 9:

### **Article 9: The Rejection of Certain Objections**
The Canons respond to critics who argue that the doctrine of predestination makes God the author of sin, unjust, or arbitrary. The article states:

> *"This same doctrine of divine election is also assailed by various objections which those who hate this doctrine are accustomed to bring up against it. But these objections, when carefully examined, are found to be false and without foundation. 1. **God is Not the Author of Sin** – The Canons reject the accusation that predestination makes God responsible for human sin. Instead, they affirm that sin arises from human rebellion, not God’s decree.
2. **God’s Desire for Salvation** – While God elects some to salvation, Scripture also teaches that He genuinely desires all people to be saved (1 Tim. 2:4). However, this does not mean all *will* be saved, as election is particular.
3. **Rejection of Arbitrariness** – The Canons deny that God’s election is based on whim or injustice. Instead, it is rooted in His sovereign grace and wisdom.
4. **Scriptural Consistency** – The article appeals to Scripture to show that God’s predestination does not contradict His holiness, justice, or love.

### **Theological Significance:**
- **Compatibilism** – The Canons uphold that God’s sovereignty and human responsibility coexist without contradiction.
- **Rejection of Hyper-Calvinism** – While affirming predestination, the Canons avoid extreme views that deny God’s general desire for salvation or the free offer of the gospel.
- **Pastoral Assurance** – The article reassures believers that election is not a cold, arbitrary decree but a gracious act of God’s love.

### **Conclusion:**
Article 9 defends the doctrine of predestination against common objections, emphasizing that it is **biblical, just, and consistent with God’s character**. It affirms that while God elects some to salvation, He remains holy, just, and desiring of all to be saved—even if not all are.

questions.response:
The **Canons of Dort** (1618–1619) are a key doctrinal statement of the **Dutch Reformed Church**, formulated in response to the **Arminian controversy**. In **Article 1 of the Second Head of Doctrine** (on Christ’s death and human redemption), the Canons teach the following about **Christ’s death and its efficacy**:

### **Key Teachings of Article 1:**
1. **Christ’s Death as a Substitutionary Atonement**
   - Christ’s death was a **satisfaction** for the sins of the elect, not for all people without exception.
   - He bore the **punishment due to sinners**, fully satisfying God’s justice.

2. **Definite (Limited) Atonement**
   - Christ’s death was **not for all people universally**, but only for the elect (those chosen by God).
   - The atonement is **efficacious**—it actually secures the salvation of those for whom Christ died.

3. **God’s Justice and Mercy Reconciled**
   - God’s justice demanded punishment for sin, but His mercy provided Christ as the substitute.
   - The atonement is **sufficient for all** (in its infinite value) but **efficient only for the elect**.

4. **Rejection of Universalism**
   - The Canons explicitly reject the Arminian view that Christ died for all people equally, making salvation possible for everyone if they believe.
   - Instead, they affirm that Christ’s death **actually redeems** those whom the Father has given Him (John 17:9).

### **Text of Article 1 (Second Head of Doctrine):**
> *"Since all men have sinned in Adam and have come under the sentence of the curse and eternal death, God would have done no injustice by leaving them all to perish and delivering them over to condemnation on account of sin, according to the words of the apostle: 'that every mouth may be stopped, and all the world may become guilty before God' (Rom. 3:19). And: 'for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God' (Rom. 3:23). And: 'For the wages of sin is death' (Rom. 6:23). But in this the love of God was manifested, that He sent His only begotten Son into the world, that whoever believes in Him should not perish but have eternal life (1 John 4:9; John 3:16). For this was the sovereign counsel and most gracious will and purpose of God the Father, that the quickening and saving efficacy of the most precious death of His Son should extend to all the elect, for bestowing upon them alone the gift of justifying faith, thereby to bring them infallibly to salvation: that is, it was the will of God that Christ by the blood of the cross, whereby He confirmed the new covenant, should effectually redeem out of every people, tribe, nation, and language, all those, and those only, who were from eternity chosen to salvation and given to Him by the Father; that He should confer upon them faith, which, together with all the other saving gifts of the Holy Spirit, He purchased for them by His death; should purge them from all sin, both original and actual, whether committed before or after believing; and having faithfully preserved them even to the end, should at last bring them, free from every spot and blemish, to the enjoyment of glory in His own presence forever."*

### **Summary of the Doctrine:**
- **Christ’s death is substitutionary**—He bore the punishment for the elect.
- **The atonement is definite**—it secures salvation for the elect, not merely makes it possible.
- **God’s justice is satisfied**—Christ’s sacrifice fully pays for sin.
- **Salvation is certain for the elect**—Christ’s death guarantees their redemption.

This article firmly rejects **Arminianism** (which teaches a universal atonement) and upholds **Calvinist soteriology** (the "L" in TULIP—**Limited Atonement** or **Definite Redemption**).

questions.response:
The **Canons of Dort** (1618–1619) are a key doctrinal statement of the **Dutch Reformed Church**, addressing the **Five Points of Calvinism** in response to the **Remonstrants (Arminians)**. **Article 8** of the **Second Head of Doctrine** (on **Christ’s Death and Human Redemption**) teaches the following about **Christ’s atonement** and its **effectiveness**:

### **Summary of Article 8:**
> *"For it was the entirely free plan and very gracious will and intention of God the Father that the enlivening and saving effectiveness of his Son’s costly death should work itself out in all his chosen ones, in order that he might grant justifying faith to them only and thereby lead them without fail to salvation. In other words, it was God’s will that Christ through the blood of the cross (by which he confirmed the new covenant) should effectively redeem from every people, tribe, nation, and language all those and only those who were chosen from eternity to salvation and given to him by the Father; that he should grant them faith (which, like the Holy Spirit’s other saving gifts, he acquired for them by his death); that he should cleanse them by his blood from all their sins, both original and actual, whether committed before or after their coming to faith; that he should faithfully preserve them to the very end; and that he should finally present them to himself, a glorious people, without spot or wrinkle."*

### **Key Teachings in Article 8:**
1. **Definite (Limited) Atonement (Particular Redemption)**
   - Christ’s death was **not a general, potential atonement** for all people without exception, but a **specific, effective atonement** for the **elect** (those chosen by God).
   - The atonement **actually secures** the salvation of the elect, not merely making it possible.
   - This is sometimes called **"limited atonement"** (though Calvinists prefer "definite atonement" or "particular redemption") because it is **intentionally limited in its scope** to the elect.

2. **The Father’s Will in Election & Atonement**
   - God the Father **purposed** that Christ’s death would **effectively redeem** only the elect.
   - The atonement is **not a mere offer** but a **certain accomplishment**—Christ’s death **actually saves** those for whom He died.

3. **Christ’s Death Secures All Necessary Benefits for the Elect**
   - Christ’s death **purchased** for the elect:
     - **Justifying faith** (not just the possibility of faith).
     - **Forgiveness of sins** (both original and actual).
     - **Preservation in faith** (perseverance of the saints).
     - **Final glorification** (presenting them spotless before God).

4. **The New Covenant in Christ’s Blood**
   - Christ’s death **confirmed the new covenant**, which is **unbreakable** for the elect.
   - Unlike the old covenant (which was conditional), the new covenant **guarantees** the salvation of all in it.

5. **Universal Language, Particular Application**
   - The article acknowledges that Christ’s redemption is **from every people, tribe, nation, and language**—but **only those chosen by the Father** (not all individuals universally).
   - This refutes the Arminian claim that Christ died equally for all people, including those who perish.

### **Contrast with Arminianism (Remonstrants)**
The Canons of Dort **reject** the Arminian view that:
- Christ’s death was a **general atonement** for all people, making salvation **possible** but not **certain** for anyone.
- The atonement **does not guarantee** the salvation of any individual, but only provides the **opportunity** for faith.
- Faith is **not a gift purchased by Christ**, but a **human choice** that determines whether the atonement is applied.

Instead, Dort teaches that:
- Christ’s death **actually saves** the elect.
- Faith is **a gift secured by Christ’s death** and **given by the Holy Spirit** to the elect.
- The atonement is **effective**, not merely potential.

### **Biblical Support Cited in the Canons**
The Canons appeal to passages such as:
- **John 10:11, 15** – *"I lay down my life for the sheep."*
- **John 17:9** – *"I am not praying for the world but for those whom you have given me."*
- **Ephesians 5:25–27** – Christ gave Himself for the church to present her holy.
- **Matthew 1:21** – *"He will save his people from their sins."*
- **Acts 20:28** – *"The church of God, which he obtained with his own blood."*

### **Conclusion**
Article 8 of the Canons of Dort teaches that **Christ’s death is a definite, effective atonement for the elect**, securing their salvation in all its aspects—faith, justification, sanctification, perseverance, and glorification. It is **not a general, potential atonement** but a **certain, accomplished redemption** for those chosen by God.

This doctrine is often summarized in the **"L" of the TULIP acronym** (*Limited Atonement*), though the Canons themselves do not use that term. Instead, they emphasize that Christ’s death **actually saves** those for whom He died.

questions.response:
The **Canons of Dort** (1618–1619), a key doctrinal statement of the **Dutch Reformed Church**, address the **corruption of man and his conversion to God** in **Article 1 of the Third and Fourth Main Points of Doctrine** (on **Human Corruption, Conversion to God, and the Way It Occurs**). Here is a summary of its teaching:

### **1. The Total Corruption of Man (Total Depravity)**
- **Original Sin:** All humanity fell in Adam’s sin, inheriting a **corrupt nature** that is **wholly inclined to evil** (Rom. 5:12; Eph. 2:1–3).
- **Spiritual Death:** Man is **dead in sin** (Eph. 2:1), unable to **understand, desire, or choose spiritual good** (1 Cor. 2:14; Rom. 8:7).
- **Bondage to Sin:** The will is **not free** but enslaved to sin (John 8:34; Rom. 6:20), making man **unable to convert himself** (Jer. 13:23; John 6:44).
- **Universal Guilt:** All people, without exception, are **under God’s wrath** (Eph. 2:3) and **deserve condemnation** (Rom. 3:10–18).

### **2. The Necessity of Divine Grace for Conversion**
- **Man Cannot Save Himself:** Because of his **total depravity**, man **cannot** by his own strength **repent, believe, or turn to God** (John 6:44; 1 Cor. 2:14).
- **God’s Sovereign Initiative:** **Conversion is entirely a work of God’s grace** (Eph. 2:8–9; Phil. 1:29). It is **not** based on human merit, foreseen faith, or free will (Rom. 9:16).
- **Regeneration Precedes Faith:** Before a person can **believe**, God must **regenerate** (give new spiritual life to) the heart (John 3:3, 5; Ezek. 36:26–27).
- **Irresistible Grace:** When God calls a person **effectually**, He **overcomes their resistance** and **grants them faith and repentance** (John 6:37, 44; Acts 16:14).

### **3. The Means of Conversion**
- **The Gospel Call:** God uses the **preaching of the Word** (Rom. 10:14–17) and the **work of the Holy Spirit** (1 Cor. 2:4–5) to bring about conversion.
- **Faith as a Gift:** **Faith is not a human work but a gift of God** (Eph. 2:8–9; Phil. 1:29), given to the elect in regeneration.
- **Repentance as God’s Work:** True repentance is **not a human achievement** but a **divine gift** (Acts 5:31; 2 Tim. 2:25).

### **Key Biblical Support**
- **Total Depravity:** Gen. 6:5; Ps. 51:5; Rom. 3:10–18; Eph. 2:1–3
- **Inability to Convert Self:** Jer. 13:23; John 6:44, 65; 1 Cor. 2:14
- **Sovereign Grace in Conversion:** John 1:13; Eph. 2:4–5; Phil. 2:13; 2 Tim. 1:9

### **Contrast with Arminianism**
The Canons of Dort **reject the Arminian view** that:
- Man has a **free will** to choose God.
- God’s grace is **resistible**.
- Faith is a **human contribution** to salvation.
Instead, Dort affirms **monergism**—salvation is **wholly God’s work**, from beginning to end.

### **Conclusion**
Article 1 of the Canons of Dort teaches that:
1. **Man is totally corrupt** and **unable to save himself**.
2. **Conversion is entirely God’s work**, not dependent on human will or effort.
3. **Regeneration precedes faith**, and God’s grace is **irresistible** in the elect.

This doctrine is foundational to **Reformed theology**, emphasizing **God’s sovereignty in salvation** and **human helplessness apart from grace**.

### **2. The Necessity of Divine Grace for Conversion**
- **Man Cannot Convert Himself**: Because of his **spiritual death**, man **cannot** by his own strength **repent, believe, or turn to God** (John 6:44; 1 Cor. 12:3).
- **Regeneration Precedes Faith**: **God must first regenerate the heart** (Ezek. 36:26–27; John 3:3–8) before a person can **believe and repent** (Acts 16:14; Eph. 2:4–5).
- **Irresistible Grace**: When God calls a person **effectually**, His grace **overcomes resistance** and **grants faith** (John 6:37, 44; Phil. 2:13).

### **3. The Means of Conversion: The Gospel and the Holy Spirit**
- **The Gospel is the Instrument**: God uses the **preaching of the Word** (Rom. 10:14–17) to **call sinners to faith**.
- **The Holy Spirit’s Work**: The Spirit **opens the heart** (Acts 16:14), **illumines the mind** (1 Cor. 2:12–14), and **grants repentance and faith** (Eph. 2:8–9; 2 Tim. 2:25).
- **Conversion is a Supernatural Act**: It is **not** a result of human effort but of **God’s sovereign grace** (John 1:13; Titus 3:5).

### **4. The Response of the Converted**
- **Faith and Repentance**: The regenerated person **believes in Christ** (Acts 16:31) and **turns from sin** (Acts 2:38).
- **Good Works Follow**: True faith **produces good works** (Eph. 2:10; James 2:17), but these are **fruits of grace**, not causes of salvation.

### **Key Biblical Support in Article 3**
- **Romans 3:10–12** – "None is righteous, no, not one; no one understands; no one seeks for God."
- **Ephesians 2:1–5** – "You were dead in your trespasses… but God made you alive."
- **John 6:44** – "No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him."
- **1 Corinthians 2:14** – "The natural person does not accept the things of the Spirit of God."

### **Contrast with Arminianism**
The Canons of Dort **reject the Arminian view** that:
- Man has a **free will** to choose God apart from grace.
- **Prevenient grace** (a universal enabling grace) makes faith possible but not certain.
- **Conversion depends on human cooperation** with grace.

Instead, Dort teaches that **salvation is entirely of God’s grace**, from beginning to end.

### **Conclusion**
Article 3 of the Canons of Dort affirms:
✔ **Total depravity** – Man is spiritually dead and unable to save himself.
✔ **Monergism** – God alone regenerates and converts the sinner.
✔ **Irresistible grace** – When God calls, He ensures the response.
✔ **Faith as a gift** – Belief is not a human work but a divine enablement.

This doctrine underscores **God’s sovereignty in salvation** and the **complete inability of man to come to God apart from grace**.

questions.response:
The **Canons of Dort** (1618–1619), a key doctrinal statement of the **Dutch Reformed Church**, address the **conversion of man and the manner thereof** in **Article 10 of the Third and Fourth Main Points of Doctrine** (on **Human Corruption and Conversion to God**). Here is the teaching in summary:

### **Article 10: The Manner of Conversion**
The Canons teach that **conversion is the work of God’s sovereign grace**, not a result of human free will or cooperation. Key points include:

1. **God’s Monergistic Work**
   - Conversion is **entirely the work of God**, who **regenerates the sinner** by the Holy Spirit, making them willing and able to believe.
   - It is **not a result of human choice** (John 1:13; Eph. 2:1, 5, 8–9).
   - The sinner is **passive** in regeneration (like a dead person being raised to life) but becomes **active** in faith and repentance afterward.

2. **The Role of the Word and Spirit**
   - God uses the **preaching of the Gospel** as the **ordinary means** of conversion (Rom. 10:14–17).
   - The **Holy Spirit** applies the Word to the heart, **opening the eyes of the blind** and **turning the will** (Acts 16:14; 2 Cor. 4:6).

3. **Irresistible Grace (Effectual Calling)**
   - When God calls a person **effectually**, they **cannot ultimately resist** (John 6:37, 44; Rom. 8:30).
   - This does not mean conversion is **forced** (as in coercion) but that God **overcomes resistance** and makes the sinner willing (Ps. 110:3).

4. **Faith as a Gift of God**
   - Faith is **not a human work** but a **gift of God** (Eph. 2:8–9; Phil. 1:29).
   - It is **not based on foreseen faith** (as in Arminianism) but is **sovereignly bestowed** by God.

5. **Repentance as a Fruit of Conversion**
   - True repentance is **not a precondition for grace** but **flows from regeneration** (Acts 5:31; 11:18).
   - The sinner, once made alive, **freely turns to God** in faith and repentance.

### **Contrast with Arminianism**
The Canons **reject the Arminian view** that:
- Conversion depends on **human free will** (as if man cooperates with grace).
- God’s grace is **resistible** (as if man can reject it despite God’s drawing).
- Faith is **a human decision** rather than a divine gift.

### **Key Scripture References**
- **John 3:3, 5–8** – Regeneration by the Spirit.
- **Ephesians 2:1–10** – Dead in sin, made alive by grace.
- **Romans 9:16** – Salvation depends on God, not man.
- **Philippians 2:13** – God works in us to will and to do.

### **Conclusion**
The Canons of Dort teach that **conversion is entirely God’s work**, from beginning to end. The sinner is **passive in regeneration** but **active in faith and repentance** as a result of God’s sovereign grace. This doctrine upholds **God’s glory in salvation** and rejects any notion of human merit or cooperation in the initial work of conversion.

questions.response:
The **Canons of Dort** (1618–1619), a key doctrinal statement of the **Dutch Reformed Church**, address the **conversion of man and the manner thereof** in **Article 11 of the Third and Fourth Main Points of Doctrine** (on **Human Corruption and Conversion to God**). Here is a summary of its teaching:

### **Article 11: The Manner of Conversion**
The Canons affirm that **God’s grace is the sole efficient cause of conversion**, working in a way that is **irresistible yet not violent**—meaning it overcomes human resistance without coercing the will in a way that violates human nature.

#### **Key Points:**
1. **God’s Sovereign Work in Conversion**
   - Conversion is **not a cooperative effort** between God and man but is **wholly the work of God’s grace**.
   - The Holy Spirit **regenerates the heart**, making the sinner willing and able to believe.
   - This work is **monergistic** (God alone acts) rather than synergistic (God and man working together).

2. **Irresistible Grace (Not Coercive)**
   - The grace of God in conversion is **irresistible** in the sense that it **effectually overcomes human resistance** (due to total depravity).
   - However, it is **not violent or coercive**—God does not force the will against its nature but **changes the heart** so that the person freely comes to Christ.
   - The sinner, though previously hostile to God, is **made willing** by the Spirit’s work (cf. Ps. 110:3; Phil. 2:13).

3. **The Role of the Preached Word**
   - The **preaching of the Gospel** is the **ordinary means** by which the Spirit works conversion.
   - The Word is **not merely an offer** but is **accompanied by the Spirit’s power** to regenerate and draw sinners to Christ (Rom. 10:17; 1 Cor. 1:21).

4. **No Merit in Man**
   - Conversion is **not based on human merit, foreseen faith, or cooperation** but solely on **God’s sovereign grace**.
   - Even the **faith by which we believe** is a **gift of God** (Eph. 2:8–9; Phil. 1:29).

5. **The Freedom of the Will Restored**
   - While the unregenerate will is **enslaved to sin** (John 8:34), in conversion, the Spirit **liberates the will** so that the person **freely and willingly** turns to Christ.
   - This is not a **natural ability** but a **supernatural work of grace**.

### **Contrast with Arminianism**
The Canons reject the **Arminian view** that:
- Conversion depends on **human free will** cooperating with grace.
- God’s grace is **resistible** (i.e., people can reject it).
- Faith is **not a gift of God** but a human decision.

Instead, Dort teaches that **God alone initiates and completes conversion**, ensuring that **all who are saved are saved by His grace alone**.

### **Scriptural Support (as cited in the Canons)**
- **Ezekiel 36:26–27** – "I will give you a new heart… and cause you to walk in my statutes."
- **John 6:44** – "No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him."
- **Philippians 2:13** – "It is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure."
- **Acts 16:14** – "The Lord opened [Lydia’s] heart to pay attention to what was said by Paul."

### **Conclusion**
Article 11 of the Canons of Dort teaches that **conversion is entirely the work of God’s grace**, which **irresistibly yet sweetly** changes the heart, making the sinner willing to believe. It is **not a human achievement** but a **divine gift**, ensuring that salvation is **by grace alone (sola gratia)** and **through faith alone (sola fide)**—faith itself being a gift from God.

The **Canons of Dort** (1618–1619) address the **perseverance of the saints** in **Fifth Head of Doctrine, Article 1**, affirming the biblical teaching that true believers, though they may struggle with sin and doubt, will **persevere in faith until the end** by God’s preserving grace. Here is the key teaching from **Article 1**:

> **"Those whom God, according to His purpose, calls to the communion of His Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, and regenerates by the Holy Spirit, He also delivers from the dominion and slavery of sin, though not entirely from the flesh and from the body of sin in this life. But He daily grants them more and more strength to fight against sin, so that they may continue in the fear of the Lord, pressing on in the way of His commandments, and may abide in the communion of His Son unto the end."**

### **Key Points from Article 1:**
1. **God’s Preserving Work** – True believers are not only called and regenerated but also **preserved by God** in their faith. Their perseverance is not due to their own strength but to God’s sovereign grace.
2. **Struggle with Sin Remains** – While believers are delivered from sin’s **dominion**, they still battle the **flesh** (remaining sinful nature) in this life.
3. **Progressive Sanctification** – God **daily strengthens** believers to resist sin, grow in holiness, and press on in obedience.
4. **Assurance of Final Perseverance** – Those who are truly united to Christ will **abide in Him until the end**, not because of their own merit, but because God keeps them.

### **Theological Significance:**
- This doctrine **rejects** the idea that a true believer can **totally and finally fall away** from faith (contrary to Arminianism).
- It **affirms** that God’s grace is **irresistible** in preserving His elect (consistent with Calvinism).
- It provides **comfort and assurance** to believers, knowing that their salvation is secure in Christ.

The Canons go on to explain in subsequent articles how God ensures this perseverance through **His Word, Spirit, and the means of grace** (e.g., preaching, sacraments, prayer).

questions.response:
The **Canons of Dort** (1618–1619) address the **perseverance of the saints** in **Fifth Head of Doctrine, Article 8**, which teaches the following key points:

### **Summary of Article 8:**
1. **God’s Preservation of the Elect**
   - Those whom God has **regenerated** and **effectually called** to faith in Christ will **certainly persevere** in that faith until the end.
   - This perseverance is **not based on their own strength** but on the **unchangeable election of God** and the **merits of Christ’s death**, which secure their salvation.

2. **The Role of the Holy Spirit**
   - The **Holy Spirit** continually works in believers, **strengthening their faith**, **preserving them from total apostasy**, and **restoring them** when they fall into sin.
   - Even when believers **stumble or fall into grievous sins**, God does not allow them to **fully and finally fall away** from grace.

3. **Assurance of Salvation**
   - Believers may **sometimes doubt** their salvation due to sin, weakness, or temptation, but God’s **faithfulness** ensures they will not be lost.
   - The **means of grace** (Word, sacraments, prayer) are used by God to **confirm and strengthen** their faith.

4. **Rejection of the Arminian View**
   - The Canons **reject the Arminian teaching** that true believers can **fall away completely and finally** from grace.
   - Instead, they affirm that **true faith cannot be lost**, though it may be weakened or tested.

### **Key Quotes from Article 8:**
> *"This perseverance of the saints does not depend on their own free will, but on the immutability of the decree of election, flowing from the free and unchangeable love of God the Father; on the efficacy of the merit and intercession of Jesus Christ; on the abiding of the Spirit and the seed of God within them; and on the nature of the covenant of grace: from all which arises also the certainty and infallibility thereof."*

> *"Although the weakness of the flesh cannot prevail against the power of God, who confirms and preserves true believers in a state of grace, yet converts are not always so influenced and actuated by the Spirit of God as not in some particular instances sinfully to deviate from the guidance of divine grace, so as to be seduced by and to comply with the lusts of the flesh; they must therefore constantly watch and pray, that they be not led into temptation."*

### **Conclusion:**
Article 8 of the Canons of Dort teaches that **true believers are kept by God’s power** and **cannot finally fall away** from salvation. While they may struggle with sin and doubt, God’s **election, Christ’s intercession, and the Holy Spirit’s work** ensure their ultimate perseverance. This doctrine provides **comfort and assurance** to believers, emphasizing that salvation is **secure in Christ**, not dependent on human effort.

The Books commonly called Apocrypha not being of Divine inspiration, are no part of the Canon (or rule) of the Scripture, and therefore are of no authority to the Church of God, nor to be any otherwise approved or made use of, then other humane writings. The Authority of the Holy Scripture for which it ought to be believed dependeth not upon the testimony of any man, or Church; but wholly upon God (who is truth it self) the Author thereof; therefore it is to be received, because it is the Word of God. We may be moved and induced by the testimony of the Church of God, to an high and reverent esteem of the Holy Scriptures; and the heavenliness of the matter, the efficacy of the Doctrine, and the Majesty of the stile, the consent of all the parts, the scope of the whole (which is to give all glory to God) the full discovery it makes of the only way of mans salvation, and many other incomparable Excellencies, and intire perfections thereof, are arguments whereby it doth abundantly evidence it self to be the Word of God; yet notwithstanding; our full perswasion, and assurance of the infallible truth, and divine authority thereof, is from the inward work of the Holy Spirit, bearing witness by and with the Word in our Hearts. The whole Councel of God concerning all things necessary for his own Glory, Mans Salvation, Faith and Life, is either expressely set down or necessarily contained in the Holy Scripture; unto which nothing at any time is to be added, whether by new Revelation of the Spirit, or traditions of men.Nevertheless we acknowledge the inward illumination of the Spirit of God, to be necessary for the saving understanding of such things as are revealed in the Word, and that there are some circumstances concerning the worship of God, and government of the Church common to humane actions and societies; which are to be ordered by the light of nature, and Christian prudence according to the general rules of the Word, which are always to be observed. All things in Scripture are not alike plain in themselves, nor alike clear unto all; yet those things which are necessary to be known, believed, and observed for Salvation, are so clearly propounded, and opened in some place of Scripture or other, that not only the learned, but the unlearned, in a due use of ordinary means, may attain to a sufficient understanding of them. The Old Testament in Hebrew, (which was the Native language of the people of God of old) and the New Testament in Greek (which at the time of the writing of it was most generally known to the Nations being immediately inspired by God, and by his singular care and Providence kept pure in all Ages, are therefore authentical; so as in all controversies of Religion the Church is finally to appeal unto them But because these original tongues are not known to all the people of God, who have a right unto, and interest in the Scriptures, and are commanded in the fear of God to read and search them, therefore they are to be translated into the vulgar language of every Nation, unto which they come, that the Word of God dwelling plentifully in all, they may worship him in an acceptable manner, and through patience and comfort of the Scriptures may have hope. The infallible rule of interpretation of Scripture is the Scripture it self: And therefore when there is a question about the true and full sense of any Scripture (which is not manifold but one) it must be searched by other places that speak more clearly. The supream judge by which all controversies of Religion are to be determined, and all Decrees of Councels, opinions of antient Writers, Doctrines of men, and private Spirits, are to be examined, and in whose sentence we are to rest, can be no other but the Holy Scripture delivered by the Spirit, into which Scripture so delivered, our faith is finally resolved.

questions.response:
The **1689 London Baptist Confession of Faith** (also called the **Second London Baptist Confession**) provides a robust and detailed doctrine of **Holy Scripture** in its **first chapter**, reflecting the Reformed and Puritan convictions of its authors. Below is a summary of its key teachings on the Bible:

---

### **1. The Divine Authority of Scripture**
- **Scripture is God’s Word**: The Confession affirms that the **66 books of the Old and New Testaments** (excluding the Apocrypha) are the **very Word of God**, written by men who were **"moved by the Holy Spirit"** (2 Peter 1:21).
- **Infallible and Inerrant**: The Bible is **"given by inspiration of God"** and is **"the only sufficient, certain, and infallible rule of all saving knowledge, faith, and obedience"** (1.1). It is **without error** in all that it affirms.
- **Supreme Authority**: Scripture is the **final authority** in all matters of faith and practice, surpassing human tradition, reason, and experience (1.4, 10).

---

### **2. The Necessity of Scripture**
- **Revelation of God’s Will**: The Bible is **necessary** for salvation because it reveals God’s plan of redemption through Christ (1.1).
- **Clarity (Perspicuity)**: The **main teachings** of Scripture (especially those concerning salvation) are **clear enough** for ordinary believers to understand, though some passages require careful study (1.7).
- **Sufficiency**: Scripture contains **all things necessary** for salvation, godliness, and Christian living—nothing needs to be added to it (1.6).

---

### **3. The Canon of Scripture**
- **Old and New Testaments**: The Confession explicitly lists the **39 books of the Old Testament** and the **27 books of the New Testament** as canonical (1.2–3).
- **Rejection of the Apocrypha**: The **deuterocanonical books** (e.g., Tobit, Judith, Maccabees) are **not part of Scripture** and are **"not of divine inspiration"** (1.3).
- **Self-Authenticating**: The Bible’s authority is **not derived from the church** but is **self-evident** to those who read it with faith (1.5).

---

### **4. The Interpretation of Scripture**
- **Scripture Interprets Scripture**: The **best interpreter of Scripture is Scripture itself**—difficult passages should be understood in light of clearer ones (1.9).
- **Role of the Holy Spirit**: The **illumination of the Holy Spirit** is necessary for true understanding (1.5, 6).
- **Rejection of Private Interpretation**: While individuals may study Scripture, the **church’s historic interpretation** (e.g., creeds, confessions) helps guard against error (1.10).

---

### **5. The Preservation of Scripture**
- **God’s Providence Over Scripture**: God has **preserved His Word** throughout history, ensuring that the **original meaning** remains accessible (1.8).
- **Translations**: While the **original Hebrew and Greek** are the ultimate standard, **faithful translations** (e.g., the KJV in the 17th century) are sufficient for the church (1.8).

---

### **6. The Use of Scripture**
- **Rule for Faith and Life**: Scripture is the **only infallible rule** for what Christians must believe and how they must live (1.1).
- **Against Human Traditions**: No **human traditions, councils, or decrees** can bind the conscience if they contradict Scripture (1.10).
- **Final Authority in Controversies**: In disputes over doctrine, **Scripture alone** is the supreme judge (1.10).

---

### **Key Differences from Other Confessions**
- **Baptist Distinctives**: While the 1689 Confession closely follows the **Westminster Confession (1646)** and the **Savoy Declaration (1658)**, it modifies some language to reflect **Baptist convictions** (e.g., believer’s baptism, congregational church government).
- **Rejection of Apocrypha**: Unlike the **Roman Catholic Church** (which includes the Apocrypha) and some Anglican traditions, the 1689 Confession **explicitly excludes** these books.
- **Emphasis on Sufficiency**: The Confession strongly affirms that **Scripture alone** is sufficient for all matters of faith and practice, a key Protestant principle.

---

### **Summary of Chapter 1 (Of the Holy Scriptures)**
> *"The Holy Scripture is the only sufficient, certain, and infallible rule of all saving knowledge, faith, and obedience... The authority of the Holy Scripture, for which it ought to be believed, dependeth not upon the testimony of any man or church, but wholly upon God (who is truth itself), the author thereof; therefore it is to be received because it is the Word of God."* (1.1, 4)

---

### **Why This Matters for Baptists Today**
The 1689 Confession’s doctrine of Scripture:
1. **Upholds the Bible as God’s inspired, inerrant Word**—not a human book.

questions.response:
The **1689 London Baptist Confession of Faith** (also known as the **Second London Baptist Confession**) presents a robust and orthodox doctrine of **God and the Holy Trinity**, closely following the Reformed tradition while affirming Baptist distinctives. Below is a summary of its key teachings on these topics:

---

### **1. The Doctrine of God (Chapter 2: "Of God and of the Holy Trinity")**
The confession begins by affirming the **existence, nature, and attributes of God** in a way that aligns with classical Christian theism:

#### **A. The Existence and Nature of God**
- **God is one** (Deut. 6:4; 1 Cor. 8:4, 6) – There is only one living and true God.
- **God is infinite in being and perfection** – He is eternal, unchangeable, incomprehensible, and almighty (Ps. 90:2; Mal. 3:6; Rom. 11:33-36).
- **God is a most pure spirit** (John 4:24) – He is invisible, without body, parts, or passions (1 Tim. 1:17; James 1:17).
- **God is self-existent and independent** – He depends on nothing outside Himself (Ex. 3:14; Acts 17:24-25).
- **God is most holy, wise, free, and absolute** – His will is sovereign, and His works are perfect (Isa. 6:3; Rom. 11:33-34; Eph. 1:11).

#### **B. The Attributes of God**
The confession lists several key attributes:
- **Eternity** – God has no beginning or end (Ps. 90:2).
- **Immutability** – He does not change (Mal. 3:6; James 1:17).
- **Omnipresence** – He is everywhere present (Ps. 139:7-10).
- **Omniscience** – He knows all things (Heb. 4:13; Ps. 147:5).
- **Omnipotence** – He is all-powerful (Gen. 17:1; Rev. 1:8).
- **Goodness, love, and mercy** – He is benevolent toward His creatures (Ex. 34:6-7; 1 John 4:8).
- **Justice and righteousness** – He is perfectly just in all His dealings (Deut. 32:4; Rom. 3:26).

#### **C. The Decrees of God**
- God has **foreordained whatsoever comes to pass** (Eph. 1:11; Rom. 11:36).
- His decrees are **eternal, wise, and holy**, not based on foreseen merit but on His own good pleasure (Rom. 9:11-18; Eph. 1:4-5).
- Yet, God is **not the author of sin** (James 1:13; 1 John 1:5), and His decrees do not violate human responsibility.

---

### **2. The Holy Trinity (Chapter 2, Paragraph 3)**
The confession strongly affirms the **doctrine of the Trinity**, following the Nicene and Athanasian Creeds:

> *"In this divine and infinite Being there are three subsistences, the Father, the Word or Son, and Holy Spirit, of one substance, power, and eternity, each having the whole divine essence, yet the essence undivided: the Father is of none, neither begotten nor proceeding; the Son is eternally begotten of the Father; the Holy Spirit proceeding from the Father and the Son; all infinite, without beginning, therefore but one God, who is not to be divided in nature and being, but distinguished by several peculiar relative properties and personal relations; which doctrine of the Trinity is the foundation of all our communion with God, and comfortable dependence on Him."*

#### **Key Points on the Trinity:**
1. **One God in Three Persons** – There is **one God** (Deut. 6:4), but He exists in **three distinct Persons**: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit (Matt. 28:19; 2 Cor. 13:14).
2. **Same Essence, Distinct Persons** – Each Person is **fully God**, sharing the same divine nature (John 1:1; Acts 5:3-4; Heb. 1:3).
3. **Eternal Relations of Origin** –
   - The **Father** is **unbegotten** (John 1:14, 18).
   - The **Son** is **eternally begotten** of the Father (John 1:18; 3:16).
   - The **Holy Spirit** **proceeds** from the Father and the Son (John 15:26; Gal. 4:6).
4. **Distinct Personal Properties** –
   - The Father **sends** the Son (John 3:16).
   - The Son **obeys** the Father (John 5:19; Phil. 2:6-8).
   - The Spirit **proceeds** from both (John 15:26).
5. **Equal in Glory and Worship** – All three Persons are **worthy of worship** (Matt. 3:16-17; Rev. 1:4-5).

#### **Biblical Support for the Trinity in the Confession:**
- **Matthew 28:19** – "Baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost."
- **2 Corinthians 13:14** – "The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Ghost, be with you all."
- **John 1:1, 14** – The Word (Son) is God and became flesh.
- **Acts 5:3-4** – Lying to the Holy Spirit is lying to God.
- **Hebrews 1:3** – The Son is the "brightness of His glory and the express image of His person."

---

### **3. Practical Implications of the Doctrine of God and the Trinity**
The confession emphasizes that the Trinity is not just a theological abstraction but has **practical significance** for the Christian life:
- **Worship** – We worship **one God in three Persons** (Matt. 4:10; Rev. 5:13).
- **Salvation** – Each Person of the Trinity plays a distinct role in redemption:
  - The **Father** elects and sends the Son (Eph. 1:3-6).
  - The **Son** accomplishes redemption (Eph. 1:7-12).
  - The **Spirit** applies redemption (Titus 3:5; Eph. 1:13-14).
- **Prayer** – We pray to the **Father**, through the **Son**, in the **Spirit** (Eph. 2:18).
- **Assurance** – The Trinity secures our salvation (2 Cor. 1:21-22; Eph. 1:13-14).

---

### **4. Comparison with Other Confessions**
The 1689 Confession’s teaching on God and the Trinity is nearly identical to:
- The **Westminster Confession of Faith (1646)** (Presbyterian)
- The **Savoy Declaration (1658)** (Congregationalist)
This reflects the **Reformed consensus** on these doctrines, with Baptists affirming the same orthodoxy while differing on ecclesiology (e.g., believer’s baptism).

---

### **5. Key Differences from Other Views**
The 1689 Confession **rejects**:
- **Modalism** (the idea that God is one Person who appears in different "modes" – Father, Son, Spirit).
- **Arianism** (the denial of the Son’s full deity).
- **Tritheism** (the belief in three separate Gods).
- **Unitarianism** (denial of the Trinity altogether).

Instead, it upholds the **Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed (381 AD)** and the **Athanasian Creed**, affirming:
- **One God in three Persons**.
- **Co-equality and co-eternity** of the Father, Son, and Spirit.
- **Distinct personal properties** (begottenness, procession).

---

### **Conclusion**
The **1689 London Baptist Confession** presents a **classical, biblical, and Reformed** doctrine of God and the Trinity. It affirms:
✅ **One God** in three Persons.
✅ **Full deity** of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
✅ **Eternal relations** (Father unbegotten, Son begotten, Spirit proceeding).
✅ **Distinct roles** in creation and redemption.
✅ **Practical importance** for worship, prayer, and salvation.

This doctrine is foundational to Baptist theology and aligns with historic Christian orthodoxy. Would you like further clarification on any aspect?

Those of mankind that are predestinated to life, God before the foundation of the world was laid, according to his eternal and immutable purpose, and the secret Councel and good pleasure of his will, hath chosen in Christ unto everlasting glory, out of his meer free grace and love; without any other thing in the creature as a condition or cause moving him thereunto. As God hath appointed the Elect unto glory, so he hath by the eternal and most free purpose of his will, fore-ordained all the means thereunto, wherefore they who are elected, being faln in Adam, are redeemed by Christ, are effectually called unto faith in Christ, by his spirit working in due season, are justifyed, adopted, sanctified, and kept by his power through faith unto salvation; neither are any other redeemed by Christ, or effectually called, justified, adopted, sanctified, and saved, but the Elect only. questions.response:
The **1689 London Baptist Confession of Faith** (also known as the **Second London Baptist Confession**) presents a **Reformed Baptist** perspective on **God’s decree**, closely following the **Westminster Confession of Faith (1646)** and the **Savoy Declaration (1658)** while maintaining distinct Baptist convictions on ecclesiology and baptism.

Here is a summary of its teaching on **God’s decree** (Chapter 3: *Of God’s Decree*):

---

### **1. God’s Eternal Decree (3.1)**
- God, from all eternity, **freely and unchangeably** ordained **whatever comes to pass** (Eph. 1:11; Rom. 9:15, 18; 11:33).
- His decree is **not based on foreseen faith, works, or any condition in creatures** (Rom. 9:11, 16; 2 Tim. 1:9).
- It is **sovereign, wise, and holy**, and He executes it in time (Isa. 46:10; Eph. 1:11).

### **2. The Decree of Election and Reprobation (3.3–7)**
- **Election**: God, before the foundation of the world, **chose some persons unto everlasting life** (Eph. 1:4; 2 Thess. 2:13).
  - This choice is **not based on foreseen merit, faith, or works** but solely on His **sovereign good pleasure** (Rom. 9:11–16; 2 Tim. 1:9).
  - The elect are **predestined to adoption, justification, sanctification, and glorification** (Rom. 8:30; Eph. 1:5).
- **Reprobation**: The rest of mankind, God was pleased to **pass over** and ordain to **dishonor and wrath** for their sin (Rom. 9:17–22; 1 Pet. 2:8).
  - This is **not an active decree to damn** but a **permissive decree**—God leaves them in their sin (Jude 4; 2 Pet. 2:12).

### **3. The Means of Election (3.6)**
- God’s decree of election is **not arbitrary** but includes the **means** by which the elect are saved:
  - **Effectual calling** (Rom. 8:30)
  - **Faith and repentance** (Eph. 2:8–10; Acts 13:48)
  - **Perseverance in grace** (Phil. 1:6; John 10:28–29)
- The elect **cannot finally fall away** (John 6:37–40; 10:28–29).

### **4. The Freedom of God’s Decree (3.1–2)**
- God’s decree **does not make Him the author of sin** (James 1:13; 1 John 1:5).
- It **does not violate human responsibility** (Acts 2:23; 4:27–28).
- God’s sovereignty and human freedom **coexist** in a way that is **mysterious but not contradictory** (Prov. 16:9; Phil. 2:12–13).

### **5. The Purpose of God’s Decree (3.5–7)**
- The ultimate end of God’s decree is **His own glory** (Eph. 1:6, 12, 14; Rom. 11:36).
- It displays **His wisdom, power, justice, mercy, and holiness** (Rom. 9:22–23; Ex. 33:18–19).

---

### **Key Differences from Other Confessions**
- The **1689 Confession** is **nearly identical** to the **Westminster Confession (3.1–8)** and the **Savoy Declaration (3.1–7)** on God’s decree.
- Unlike **Lutheran or Arminian** views, it **rejects conditional election** (election based on foreseen faith).
- Unlike **hyper-Calvinism**, it **affirms the free offer of the gospel** (3.7) and the **duty of all to repent and believe** (14.1–2).

### **Scriptural Support in the Confession**
The confession cites key passages such as:
- **Ephesians 1:4–5, 11** (election according to God’s purpose)
- **Romans 9:11–23** (God’s sovereign choice and mercy)
- **2 Timothy 1:9** (grace given before time began)
- **1 Peter 1:2** (election according to foreknowledge)
- **Acts 13:48** (appointed to eternal life)

---

### **Conclusion**
The **1689 London Baptist Confession** teaches that:
1. **God’s decree is eternal, unchangeable, and sovereign.**
2. **Election is unconditional, based on God’s good pleasure.**
3. **Reprobation is a passive decree, leaving the non-elect in their sin.**
4. **The elect are saved through means (faith, repentance, perseverance).**
5. **God’s decree glorifies Himself in all things.**

This reflects a **high Calvinist** view of predestination, consistent with **Reformed theology** while maintaining distinct Baptist ecclesiology.
