questions.response:
The **1689 London Baptist Confession of Faith** (also known as the **Second London Baptist Confession**) provides a robust and Reformed understanding of **divine providence** in **Chapter 5**, which is closely aligned with the Westminster Confession of Faith (1646) and the Savoy Declaration (1658). Here is a summary of its key teachings:

---

### **Chapter 5: Of Divine Providence**
#### **1. God’s Sovereign Governance of All Things**
> *"God the good Creator of all things, in His infinite power and wisdom, upholds, directs, disposes, and governs all creatures and things, from the greatest even to the least, by His most wise and holy providence, to the end for which they were created, according unto His infallible foreknowledge, and the free and immutable counsel of His own will; to the praise of the glory of His wisdom, power, justice, infinite goodness, and mercy."* (5.1)

- **God’s Sustaining Power**: God not only created all things but **actively upholds and governs** them (Heb. 1:3; Col. 1:17).
- **Comprehensive Control**: His providence extends to **all creatures and events**, from the greatest (angels, nations) to the smallest (sparrows, hairs of our head) (Matt. 10:29-30).
- **Purposeful Governance**: Everything is directed toward **God’s predetermined ends** (Eph. 1:11; Rom. 11:36).
- **Based on His Decrees**: Providence flows from God’s **infallible foreknowledge** and **immutable counsel** (Acts 2:23; 4:27-28).

#### **2. God’s Ordinary and Extraordinary Works**
> *"Although in relation to the foreknowledge and decree of God, the first cause, all things come to pass immutably and infallibly; so that there is not anything befalls any by chance, or without His providence; yet by the same providence He ordereth them to fall out according to the nature of second causes, either necessarily, freely, or contingently."* (5.2)

- **Primary and Secondary Causes**:
  - **Primary Cause**: God is the **ultimate cause** of all things (Eph. 1:11).
  - **Secondary Causes**: God ordinarily works through **natural means** (e.g., laws of nature, human choices, historical events).
- **No True "Chance"**: Nothing happens by **blind fate** or **randomness**—all is under God’s sovereign control (Prov. 16:33).
- **Compatibility with Human Freedom**:
  - God’s providence does not **coerce** free agents (e.g., humans, angels) but **ordains** their choices (Acts 2:23; 4:27-28).
  - Even **sinful actions** (e.g., Joseph’s brothers, Judas’ betrayal) are under God’s control but not His moral approval (Gen. 50:20; Acts 2:23).

#### **3. God’s Special Providence Over His People**
> *"God, in His ordinary providence maketh use of means, yet is free to work without, above, and against them at His pleasure."* (5.3)

- **Means and Miracles**:
  - God **ordinarily** works through **means** (e.g., prayer, preaching, medicine, human effort).
  - Yet He is **not bound** by them and can work **supernaturally** (e.g., miracles, direct intervention) (Isa. 55:8-9; Dan. 3:17-18).
- **Special Care for the Elect**:
  - God’s providence is **particular** toward His people, ensuring their **preservation and salvation** (Rom. 8:28-30; Phil. 1:6).
  - Even **suffering** is used for their good (Rom. 8:28; Gen. 50:20).

#### **4. The Mystery of Providence and Human Responsibility**
> *"The almighty power, unsearchable wisdom, and infinite goodness of God, so far manifest themselves in His providence, that His determinate counsel extendeth itself even to the first fall, and all other sinful actions both of angels and men; and that not by a bare permission, which also He most wisely and powerfully boundeth, and otherwise ordereth and governeth, in a manifold dispensation to His most holy ends; yet so, as the sinfulness of their acts proceedeth only from the creatures, and not from God, who, being most holy and righteous, neither is nor can be the author or approver of sin."* (5.4)

- **God’s Sovereignty Over Sin**:
  - God **ordains** sinful actions (e.g., the Fall, Judas’ betrayal) **without being the author of sin** (James 1:13-14).
  - He **permits** evil but **restrains and directs** it for His purposes (Job 1:12; 2:6).
- **Human Responsibility**:
  - Sinners are **fully accountable** for their actions (Acts 2:23; 4:27-28).
  - God’s decree does not **violate human freedom** but **establishes it** (Prov. 16:9; Phil. 2:12-13).
- **No Moral Blame on God**:
  - God is **holy and just**—He **hates sin** and **judges it** (Hab. 1:13; Rom. 9:14-24).

#### **5. The Comfort of Providence for Believers**
> *"The most wise, righteous, and gracious God doth oftentimes leave for a season His own children to manifold temptations and the corruptions of their own hearts, to chastise them for their former sins, or to discover unto them the hidden strength of corruption and deceitfulness of their hearts, that they may be humbled; and to raise them to a more close and constant dependence for their support upon Himself; and to make them more watchful against all future occasions of sin, and for other just and holy ends."* (5.5)

- **Trials and Discipline**:
  - God **allows** suffering in the lives of believers for **sanctification** (Heb. 12:5-11; James 1:2-4).
  - Even **temptations** are under His control (1 Cor. 10:13).
- **Purpose in Suffering**:
  - To **humble** us (2 Cor. 12:7-10).
  - To **increase dependence** on God (Ps. 119:67, 71).
  - To **refine faith** (1 Pet. 1:6-7).

> *"So that whatsoever befalls any of His elect is by His appointment, for His glory, and their good."* (5.6)

- **Assurance for the Elect**:
  - All things work together for **good** (Rom. 8:28).
  - God’s providence is **purposeful**—for His **glory** and our **good**.

#### **6. The Final Judgment and Providence**
> *"As for those wicked and ungodly men whom God, as the righteous judge, for former sin doth blind and harden; from them He not only withholdeth His grace, whereby they might have been enlightened in their understandings, and wrought upon their hearts; but sometimes also withdraweth the gifts which they had, and exposeth them to such objects as their corruption makes occasion of sin; and withal, gives them over to their own lusts, the temptations of the world, and the power of Satan, whereby it comes to pass that they harden themselves, under those means which God useth for the softening of others."* (5.6)

- **Judicial Hardening**:
  - God **justly** hardens the wicked (Rom. 1:24-28; 9:17-18).
  - He **withholds grace** from those who reject Him (Matt. 13:13-15).
  - Yet, they are **fully responsible** for their rebellion (Rom. 1:20-21).

---

### **Key Theological Emphases**
1. **Sovereignty & Control**: God governs **all things**—creation, history, salvation, and even sin—without being the author of evil.
2. **Compatibilism**: Human freedom and divine sovereignty **coexist** (Acts 2:23; Phil. 2:12-13).
3. **Purpose in Suffering**: Trials are **ordained for good** (Rom. 8:28; James 1:2-4).
4. **Comfort for Believers**: Providence assures that **nothing happens by chance**—all is under God’s loving care (Ps. 139:16; Matt. 6:25-34).

questions.reference_answer: The distance between God and the Creature is so great, that although reasonable Creatures do owe obedience unto him as their Creator, yet they could never have attained the reward of Life, but by some voluntary condescension on Gods part, which he hath been pleased to express, by way of Covenant. Moreover Man having brought himself under the curse of the Law by his fall, it pleased the Lord to make a Covenant of Grace wherein he freely offereth unto Sinners, Life and Salvation by Jesus Christ, requiring of them Faith in him, that they may be saved; and promising to give unto all those that are ordained unto eternal Life, his holy Spirit, to make them willing, and able to believe. This Covenant is revealed in the Gospel; first of all to Adam in the promise of Salvation by the seed of the woman, and afterwards by farther steps, untill the full discovery thereof was compleated in the new Testament; and it is founded in that Eternal Covenant transaction, that was between the Father and the Son, about the Redemption of the Elect; and it is alone by the Grace of this Covenant, that all of the posterity of fallen Adam, that ever were saved, did obtain life and a blessed immortality; Man being now utterly uncapable of acceptance with God upon those terms, on which Adam stood in his state of innocency.

questions.response:
The **1689 London Baptist Confession of Faith** (also called the **Second London Baptist Confession**) presents a **covenantal theology** that is deeply rooted in Reformed Baptist thought, drawing heavily from the **Westminster Confession of Faith (1646)** and the **Savoy Declaration (1658)** while adapting it to Baptist distinctives (particularly believer’s baptism and a congregational ecclesiology).

Here’s a breakdown of its teaching on **God’s covenant(s)**:

---

### **1. The Covenant of Works (Pre-Fall)**
The Confession affirms the **Covenant of Works** (or **Covenant of Life**) made with Adam before the Fall, though it does not use the term explicitly. Instead, it describes Adam’s relationship with God in covenantal terms:

> **"The distance between God and the creature is so great, that although reasonable creatures do owe obedience to Him as their Creator, yet they could never have attained the reward of life but by some voluntary condescension on God’s part, which He hath been pleased to express by way of covenant."** (7.1)

- **Key Points:**
  - God entered into a **covenant of life** with Adam, promising **eternal life** upon perfect obedience.
  - Adam’s failure in this covenant brought **sin and death** upon humanity (6.1–3).
  - This covenant establishes the **legal basis** for Christ’s obedience as the **second Adam** (Rom. 5:12–21).

---

### **2. The Covenant of Grace (Post-Fall)**
The Confession strongly emphasizes the **Covenant of Grace** as the means by which God redeems His elect through Christ. Unlike the **Covenant of Works**, this covenant is **unconditional** (based on God’s sovereign grace, not human merit).

> **"This covenant is revealed in the gospel; first of all to Adam in the promise of salvation by the seed of the woman, and afterwards by farther steps, until the full discovery thereof was completed in the New Testament."** (7.3)

- **Key Points:**
  - The **Covenant of Grace** was **administered differently** in different epochs (Old vs. New Testament), but it is **one covenant** with the same substance (7.5–6).
  - **Old Testament administrations** (Noahic, Abrahamic, Mosaic, Davidic) were **types and shadows** pointing to Christ (Heb. 8–10).
  - The **New Covenant** (Jer. 31:31–34; Heb. 8:6–13) is the **fulfillment** of the Covenant of Grace, bringing **fuller revelation, better promises, and inward transformation** (7.3–4).
  - **Baptists differ from Presbyterians** in that they see the **New Covenant as exclusively for the elect** (not a mixed covenant like the Mosaic), which is why they reject infant baptism (29.1–2).

---

### **3. The New Covenant as the Fulfillment of the Covenant of Grace**
The Confession teaches that the **New Covenant** is the **final and perfect administration** of the Covenant of Grace:

> **"This covenant is made with Christ as the second Adam, and in Him with all the elect as His seed."** (7.3)

- **Key Distinctions from the Old Covenant:**
  - **Inward transformation:** The law is written on the heart (Jer. 31:33; Heb. 8:10).
  - **Forgiveness of sins:** All in the New Covenant have their sins forgiven (Jer. 31:34; Heb. 8:12).
  - **Direct knowledge of God:** All in the New Covenant know the Lord (Jer. 31:34).
  - **Eternal security:** The New Covenant is **unbreakable** (Heb. 8:13; 10:14–18).

- **Baptist Distinctive:**
  - Since the New Covenant is **only for the regenerate**, **only believers (and their children, if they profess faith) are proper subjects of baptism** (29.1–2). This contrasts with paedobaptist views that see the New Covenant as a continuation of the Abrahamic covenant (including infants).

---

### **4. Christ as the Mediator of the Covenant**
The Confession teaches that **Christ is the Mediator of the Covenant of Grace**, fulfilling all its conditions on behalf of the elect:

> **"The Lord Jesus, by His perfect obedience and sacrifice of Himself, which He through the eternal Spirit once offered up unto God, hath fully satisfied the justice of God, procured reconciliation, and purchased an everlasting inheritance in the kingdom of heaven for all those whom the Father hath given unto Him."** (8.5)

- **Christ’s work includes:**
  - **Active obedience** (fulfilling the Covenant of Works on behalf of the elect).
  - **Passive obedience** (dying for their sins).
  - **Intercession** (Heb. 7:25; 9:24).

---

### **5. The Covenant and the Church**
The Confession links the **New Covenant** to the **visible church**, but with a **Baptist understanding of church membership**:

> **"The catholic or universal church, which (with respect to the internal work of the Spirit and truth of grace) may be called invisible, consists of the whole number of the elect, that have been, are, or shall be gathered into one, under Christ, the head thereof."** (26.1)

- **Key Points:**
  - The **invisible church** = all the elect (past, present, future).
  - The **visible church** = those who profess faith and are baptized (26.2).
  - **Baptism is the sign of entrance into the visible church** (29.1–2).
  - The **Lord’s Supper** is a **covenant meal** for those in the New Covenant (30.1–2).

---

### **6. Differences from Presbyterian Covenantal Theology**
While the 1689 Confession shares much with **Westminster** (Presbyterian) and **Savoy** (Congregationalist) confessions, it differs in key ways:

| **Issue**               | **1689 Baptist Confession** | **Westminster/Savoy** |
|-------------------------|----------------------------|-----------------------|
| **Nature of the New Covenant** | Exclusively for the elect (Jer. 31:31–34) | Includes believers and their children (like the Abrahamic covenant) |
| **Baptism** | Only for believers (credobaptism) | For believers and their infants (paedobaptism) |
| **Church Membership** | Only regenerate, baptized believers | Includes infants of believers (via covenant) |
| **Old Covenant** | A **temporary, typological** administration of the Covenant of Grace | A **mixed covenant** (some elect, some not) with continuing obligations |

---

### **7. Practical Implications of the 1689’s Covenant Theology**
1. **Salvation is by grace alone** – The Covenant of Grace is **unconditional**, based on God’s election (3.5; 10.1–2).
2. **Christ is the only Mediator** – No other covenant (e.g., Mosaic) can save; only Christ’s work secures redemption (8.1–2).
3. **The New Covenant is better** – It brings **full forgiveness, inward transformation, and eternal security** (7.3–4; Heb. 8:6–13).
4. **Baptism is for believers only** – Since the New Covenant is **only for the regenerate**, only those who profess faith are baptized (29.1–2).
5. **The church is a covenant community** – Membership is restricted to those who have entered the New Covenant through faith and baptism (26.2).

---

### **Conclusion**
The **1689 London Baptist Confession** presents a **Reformed Baptist covenantal theology** that:
- Affirms the **Covenant of Works** (with Adam).
- Teaches the **Covenant of Grace** as the **one redemptive covenant** administered differently in history.
- Sees the **New Covenant** as the **final, perfect fulfillment** of the Covenant of Grace, **exclusively for the elect**.
- Rejects **paedobaptism** because the New Covenant is **only for believers**, not a mixed covenant including infants.
- Emphasizes **Christ as the Mediator** who fulfills all covenant conditions for His people.

This framework shapes **Baptist ecclesiology, soteriology, and sacramentology**, distinguishing it from Presbyterian and Anglican covenantal views while maintaining a strong Reformed foundation.

questions.question: What does the 1689 London Baptist Confession teach about christ the mediator?
questions.reference_answer: It pleased God in his eternal purpose, to chuse and ordain the Lord Jesus his only begotten Son, according to the Covenant made between them both, to be the Mediator between God and Man; the Prophet, Priest and King; Head and Saviour of his Church, the heir of all things, and judge of the world: Unto whom he did from all Eternity give a people to be his seed, and to be by him in time redeemed, called, justified, sanctified, and glorified. The Son of God, the second Person in the Holy Trinity, being very and eternal God, the brightness of the Fathers glory, of one substance and equal with him: who made the World, who upholdeth and governeth all things he hath made: did when the fullness of time was come take unto him mans nature, with all the Essential properties, and common infirmities thereof, yet without sin: being conceived by the Holy Spirit in the Womb of the Virgin Mary, the Holy Spirit coming down upon her, and the power of the most High overshadowing her, and so was made of a Woman, of the Tribe of Judah, of the Seed of Abraham, and David according to the Scriptures: So that two whole, perfect, and distinct natures, were inseparably joined together in one Person: without conversion, composition, or confusion: which Person is very God, and very Man; yet one Christ, the only Mediator between God and Man. The Lord Jesus in his humane nature thus united to the divine, in the Person of the Son, was sanctified, and anointed with the Holy Spirit, above measure; having in him all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge; in whom it pleased the Father that all fullness should dwell: To the end that being holy, harmless, undefiled, and full of Grace, and Truth, he might be throughly furnished to execute the office of a Mediator, and Surety; which office he took not upon himself, but was thereunto called by his Father; who also put all power and judgement in his hand, and gave him Commandement to execute the same. This office the Lord Jesus did most willingly undertake, which that he might discharge he was made under the Law, and did perfectly fulfill it, and underwent the punishment due to us, which we should have born and suffered, being made Sin and a Curse for us: enduring most grievous sorrows in his Soul; and most painful sufferings in his body; was crucified, and died, and remained in the state of the dead; yet saw no corruption: on the third day he arose from the dead, with the same body in which he suffered; with which he also ascended into heaven: and there sitteth at the right hand of his Father, making intercession; and shall return to judge Men and Angels, at the end of the World. The Lord Jesus by his perfect obedience and sacrifice of himself, which he through the Eternal Spirit once offered up unto God, hath fully satisfied the Justice of God, procured reconciliation, and purchased an Everlasting inheritance in the Kingdom of Heaven, for all those whom the Father hath given unto him. Although the price of Redemption was not actually paid by Christ, till after his Incarnation, yet the vertue, efficacy, and benefit thereof were communicated to the Elect in all ages successively, from the beginning of the World, in and by those Promises, Types, and Sacrifices, wherein he was revealed, and signified to be the Seed of the Woman, which should bruise the Serpents head; and the Lamb slain from the foundation of the World: Being the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever. Christ in the work of Mediation acteth according to both natures, by each nature doing that which is proper to it self; yet by reason of the Unity of the Person, that which is proper to one nature, is sometimes in Scripture attributed to the Person denominated by the other nature. To all those for whom Christ hath obtained eternal redemption, he doth certainly, and effectually apply, and communicate the same; making intercession for them, uniting them to himself by his spirit, revealing unto them, in and by the word, the mystery of salvation; perswading them to believe, and obey; governing their hearts by his word and spirit, and overcoming all their enemies by his Almighty power, and wisdom; in such manner, and wayes as are most consonant to his wonderful, and unsearchable dispensation; and all of free, and absolute Grace, without any condition foreseen in them, to procure it. This office of Mediator between God and Man, is proper onely to Christ, who is the Prophet, Priest, and King of the Church of God; and may not be either in whole, or any part thereof transfer'd from him to any other. This number and order of Offices is necessary; for in respect of our ignorance, we stand in need of his prophetical Office; and in respect of our alienation from God, and imperfection of the best of our services, we need his Priestly office, to reconcile us, and present us acceptable unto God: and in respect our averseness, and utter inability to return to God, and for our rescue, and security from our spiritual adversaries, we need his Kingly office, to convince, subdue, draw, uphold, deliver, and preserve us to his Heavenly Kingdome.

questions.response:
The **1689 London Baptist Confession of Faith** (also known as the **Second London Baptist Confession**) provides a robust and detailed exposition of **Christ the Mediator** in **Chapter 8**, which is titled *"Of Christ the Mediator."* This chapter aligns closely with the **Westminster Confession of Faith (1646)** and the **Savoy Declaration (1658)**, reflecting Reformed and Particular Baptist theology.

Here is a summary of its key teachings on **Christ the Mediator**:

---

### **1. The Necessity of a Mediator**
- **8.1** – God, in His infinite wisdom and grace, appointed **Jesus Christ, the eternal Son of God**, to be the **Mediator between God and man** (1 Tim. 2:5; John 14:6).
- This mediation was **necessary** because of humanity’s **fall into sin**, which made reconciliation with God impossible apart from a divine mediator (Rom. 5:12-19; Heb. 9:15).

---

### **2. The Person of Christ: Fully God and Fully Man**
- **8.2** – Christ, as the Mediator, is **both God and man in two distinct natures, yet one person forever**.
  - **Divine Nature**: He is the **eternal Son of God**, of the same substance (homoousios) and equal with the Father (John 1:1, 14; Col. 2:9).
  - **Human Nature**: He took upon Himself a **true human body and a reasonable soul** (Heb. 2:14-17; Phil. 2:7).
  - **Hypostatic Union**: These two natures are **united in one person**, without mixture, confusion, or separation (John 1:14; 1 Tim. 3:16).
- This union was **necessary** for Him to be a **qualified mediator**—able to represent both God and man (Heb. 2:17; 4:15).

---

### **3. The Offices of Christ: Prophet, Priest, and King**
- **8.10** – Christ executes the office of **Mediator in three distinct ways**:
  1. **Prophet** – He reveals God’s will to His people by His Word and Spirit (Deut. 18:18; John 1:18; Acts 3:22).
  2. **Priest** – He offered Himself as a **sacrifice for sin** and continually intercedes for His people (Heb. 7:25; 9:24-28).
  3. **King** – He rules over His church, subdues enemies, and defends His people (Ps. 2:6; Matt. 28:18; Eph. 1:22).

---

### **4. The Work of Christ: His Humiliation and Exaltation**
- **8.4** – Christ’s mediatorial work involved **two states**:
  1. **Humiliation** – He was **born under the law**, lived in poverty, suffered, and died on the cross (Phil. 2:6-8; Gal. 4:4).
  2. **Exaltation** – He rose from the dead, ascended into heaven, and is seated at the right hand of God (Phil. 2:9-11; Heb. 1:3).
- His **obedience and sacrifice** fully satisfied God’s justice, securing **eternal redemption** for His people (Heb. 9:12; Rom. 3:25-26).

---

### **5. Christ’s Atonement: Particular and Effectual**
- **8.5** – Christ’s death was a **substitutionary atonement** for the sins of the **elect** (Eph. 5:25; John 10:11).
- **8.6** – His sacrifice was **sufficient for all** but **efficient only for the elect** (John 17:9; Matt. 1:21).
- **8.8** – Christ’s intercession ensures that all for whom He died will **certainly be saved** (Rom. 8:34; Heb. 7:25).

---

### **6. Christ’s Mediatorial Role in Salvation**
- **8.9** – Christ’s mediation includes:
  - **Purchasing redemption** (Eph. 1:7).
  - **Applying redemption** through the Holy Spirit (Titus 3:5-6).
  - **Preserving His people** to the end (John 10:28-29).
- **8.10** – He is the **only mediator** between God and man (1 Tim. 2:5), and no one comes to the Father except through Him (John 14:6).

---

### **7. The Perfection and Sufficiency of Christ’s Work**
- **8.11** – Christ’s mediation is **perfect and complete**, needing no addition (Heb. 10:14).
- **8.12** – His work is **eternally effective**, securing the salvation of all who trust in Him (Heb. 7:24-25).

---

### **Key Differences from Other Confessions**
While the **1689 Confession** closely follows the **Westminster Confession** on Christ’s mediation, it differs in its **Baptist distinctives**, particularly in:
- **Covenant Theology** (Chapter 7) – Emphasizing **believer’s baptism** and a **new covenant** framework.
- **Church Polity** (Chapters 26-30) – Rejecting infant baptism and episcopal hierarchy.

However, on **Christ the Mediator**, it remains **fully Reformed**, affirming:
- **Sola Christus** (Christ alone as Mediator).
- **Definite Atonement** (Christ died for the elect).
- **The Hypostatic Union** (two natures in one person).

---

### **Conclusion**
The **1689 London Baptist Confession** presents Christ as the **only, perfect, and sufficient Mediator**—fully God and fully man, whose work of **propitiation, intercession, and reign** secures the salvation of His people. It upholds **Reformed orthodoxy** while maintaining **Baptist distinctives** in ecclesiology and covenant theology.

questions.response:
The **1689 London Baptist Confession of Faith** (also known as the **Second London Baptist Confession**) provides a clear and robust Reformed Baptist perspective on **effectual calling**, aligning closely with the broader Reformed tradition while maintaining distinct Baptist convictions. Here’s what it teaches on this doctrine:

---

### **Key Passages from the 1689 Confession on Effectual Calling**
The confession addresses effectual calling primarily in **Chapter 10: "Of Effectual Calling"** (which mirrors the Westminster Confession’s Chapter 10). Here are the key points:

#### **1. Definition of Effectual Calling**
> *"Those whom God hath predestinated unto life, He is pleased in His appointed and accepted time, effectually to call, by His Word and Spirit, out of that state of sin and death in which they are by nature, to grace and salvation by Jesus Christ..."* (10.1)

- **Effectual calling** is the **divine summons** by which God irresistibly draws His elect to Christ.
- It is **distinct from the general call of the gospel** (which goes out to all people but is often rejected).
- It is **monergistic** (God alone acts) and **effectual** (it always results in salvation).

#### **2. The Means of Effectual Calling**
> *"...enlightening their minds spiritually and savingly to understand the things of God; taking away their heart of stone, and giving unto them a heart of flesh; renewing their wills, and by His almighty power determining them to that which is good, and effectually drawing them to Jesus Christ; yet so as they come most freely, being made willing by His grace."* (10.1)

- **The Word of God** (preached or read) is the **instrument** God uses.
- **The Holy Spirit** applies the Word to the heart, **regenerating** the sinner (giving new life).
- **Key effects of effectual calling:**
  - **Enlightenment** (spiritual understanding of the gospel).
  - **Heart transformation** (from stone to flesh—Ezekiel 36:26).
  - **Will renewal** (the sinner’s will is freed from bondage to sin and made willing to believe).
  - **Irresistible drawing** (John 6:44—no one comes to Christ unless the Father draws them).

#### **3. The Freedom of the Will in Effectual Calling**
> *"This effectual call is of God’s free and special grace alone, not from anything at all foreseen in man, nor from any power or agency in the creature, being wholly passive therein, until, being quickened and renewed by the Holy Spirit, he is thereby enabled to answer this call, and to embrace the grace offered and conveyed in it."* (10.2)

- **Man is passive** in regeneration (Ephesians 2:1, 5—"dead in trespasses").
- **God’s grace is the sole cause**—not human merit, foreseen faith, or natural ability.
- **The sinner is made willing** (Psalm 110:3—"Your people shall be willing in the day of Your power").
- **True freedom** is restored when the sinner is enabled to respond in faith.

#### **4. The Certainty of Effectual Calling**
> *"Elect infants dying in infancy are regenerated and saved by Christ through the Spirit, who worketh when, and where, and how He pleaseth. So also are all elect persons who are incapable of being outwardly called by the ministry of the Word."* (10.3)

- **Effectual calling is not limited to those who hear the gospel preached.**
  - **Infants** (elect infants who die in infancy) are saved by Christ through the Spirit’s work.
  - **Those incapable of hearing** (e.g., the mentally disabled) are also included in God’s saving work.
- This affirms **God’s sovereignty in salvation** beyond human means.

#### **5. The Irresistibility of Effectual Calling**
> *"Others not elected, although they may be called by the ministry of the Word, and may have some common operations of the Spirit, yet not being effectually drawn by the Father, they neither will nor can truly come to Christ, and therefore cannot be saved..."* (10.4)

- **The non-elect** may hear the gospel and even experience **common grace** (conviction, moral influence), but they **cannot** come to Christ unless effectually called.
- **Resistance to the gospel** is not due to a lack of power in God’s call but to **human depravity** (John 6:44, 65; Romans 8:7-8).
- **Effectual calling is irresistible**—those whom God calls **will** come to Christ (John 6:37).

---

### **Key Theological Emphases**
1. **Monergism** – Salvation is **entirely God’s work** from beginning to end (Ephesians 2:8-9; Philippians 1:6).
2. **Regeneration Precedes Faith** – The sinner is **born again** before believing (John 3:3-8; 1 John 5:1).
3. **Irresistible Grace** – God’s call **cannot be thwarted** by human resistance (Romans 9:16).
4. **Particular Redemption** – Effectual calling is **only for the elect** (John 10:14-16, 27-29).
5. **The Means of Grace** – While God is sovereign, He **ordinarily uses the preaching of the Word** as the means of calling (Romans 10:14-17).

---

### **Comparison with Other Confessions**
- **Westminster Confession (1646)** – Nearly identical in wording (Chapter 10), reflecting shared Reformed theology.
- **1644 London Baptist Confession** – Earlier Baptist confession with less detail on effectual calling.
- **New Hampshire Confession (1833)** – Later Baptist confession with a softer stance on election and calling.

---

### **Practical Implications**
1. **Humility in Evangelism** – We preach the gospel **knowing that only God can open hearts** (Acts 16:14).
2. **Assurance for Believers** – If you have come to Christ, it is because **God called you** (Romans 8:30).
3. **Comfort in Sovereignty** – God’s call is **not dependent on human effort** (2 Timothy 1:9).
4. **Warning Against Presumption** – Those who reject the gospel **prove they were never called** (1 John 2:19).

---

### **Conclusion**
The **1689 London Baptist Confession** teaches that **effectual calling** is the **sovereign, gracious, and irresistible work of God** by which He brings His elect to salvation through the Word and Spirit. It is **monergistic, particular, and certain**, ensuring that all whom God calls will come to Christ. This doctrine underscores **God’s absolute sovereignty in salvation** while affirming the **necessity of the preached gospel** as the ordinary means of calling.

questions.question: What does the 1689 London Baptist Confession teach about justification?
questions.reference_answer: Those whom God Effectually calleth, he also freely justifieth, not by infusing Righteousness into them, but by pardoning their sins, and by accounting, and accepting their Persons as Righteous; not for any thing wrought in them, or done by them, but for Christ's sake alone, not by imputing faith it self, the act of beleiving, or any other evangelical obedience to them, as their Righteousness; but by imputing Christs active obedience unto the whole Law, and passive obedience in his death, for their whole and sole Righteousnnss, they receiving, and resting on him, and his Righteousness, by Faith; which faith they have not of themselves, it is the gift of God. Faith thus receiving and resting on Christ, and his Righteousness, is the alone instrument of Justification: yet it is not alone in the person justified, but is ever accompanied with all other saving Graces, and is no dead faith, but worketh by love. questions.response:
The **1689 London Baptist Confession of Faith** (also called the **Second London Baptist Confession**) provides a robust Reformed Baptist perspective on **justification**, closely aligning with the Westminster Confession of Faith (1646) and the Savoy Declaration (1658) while maintaining distinct Baptist convictions on ecclesiology and baptism. Below is a summary of its key teachings on justification:

---

### **1. Definition of Justification (Chapter 11: "Of Justification")**
The confession defines justification as:
> *"Those whom God effectually calleth, He also freely justifieth: not by infusing righteousness into them, but by pardoning their sins, and by accounting and accepting their persons as righteous; not for anything wrought in them, or done by them, but for Christ’s sake alone; not by imputing faith itself, the act of believing, or any other evangelical obedience to them, as their righteousness; but by imputing Christ’s active obedience unto the whole law, and passive obedience in His death for their whole and sole righteousness, they receiving and resting on Him and His righteousness by faith, which faith they have not of themselves; it is the gift of God."* (11.1)

**Key Points:**
- **Legal Declaration, Not Infusion:** Justification is a **forensic (legal) act** of God, not a process of moral transformation (which is sanctification). God declares the sinner righteous, not by making them inherently righteous.
- **Double Imputation:**
  - **Christ’s Righteousness Imputed:** God credits (imputes) the **perfect obedience and sacrificial death of Christ** to the believer’s account.
  - **Sins Imputed to Christ:** The believer’s sins were imputed to Christ on the cross (2 Cor. 5:21).
- **Faith as the Instrument:** Faith is the **instrument** by which the believer receives Christ’s righteousness, not the **ground** of justification. Faith itself is a gift of God (Eph. 2:8–9).
- **Not Based on Works:** Justification is **not** based on any inherent righteousness, good works, or religious observance (Rom. 3:28; Gal. 2:16).

---

### **2. The Ground of Justification (11.1–2)**
The confession emphasizes that justification is **solely** based on:
- **Christ’s Active Obedience:** His perfect fulfillment of the law (Matt. 3:15; Rom. 5:19).
- **Christ’s Passive Obedience:** His sacrificial death on the cross (Isa. 53:5–6; Rom. 3:25).
- **God’s Free Grace:** Justification is a **gift** (Rom. 3:24), not earned by human merit.

> *"God did from all eternity decree to justify all the elect, and Christ did in the fullness of time die for their sins, and rise again for their justification; nevertheless, they are not justified personally until the Holy Spirit doth in due time actually apply Christ unto them."* (11.4)

---

### **3. The Time of Justification (11.4)**
- **Eternal Decree:** God **decreed** to justify the elect from eternity (Eph. 1:4).
- **Historical Basis:** Christ’s death and resurrection **secured** justification (Rom. 4:25).
- **Personal Application:** Justification is **applied** to the believer when the Holy Spirit regenerates and unites them to Christ by faith (Titus 3:5–7).

---

### **4. The Role of Faith (11.2)**
- **Faith Alone (Sola Fide):** Justification is received **by faith alone**, not by works (Rom. 3:28).
- **Faith as a Gift:** Faith is **not a meritorious work** but a gift of God (Eph. 2:8–9).
- **Faith’s Object:** True faith **rests on Christ alone** (John 3:16; Acts 16:31).

> *"Faith thus receiving and resting on Christ and His righteousness, is the alone instrument of justification; yet it is not alone in the person justified, but is ever accompanied with all other saving graces, and is no dead faith, but worketh by love."* (11.2)

**Note:** While faith is the **only instrument** of justification, it is **never alone** in the believer—it produces good works (James 2:17). However, works are the **fruit** of justification, not its **cause**.

---

### **5. The Permanence of Justification (11.5)**
- **Once Justified, Always Justified:** Justification is **eternally secure** because it is based on Christ’s finished work, not human performance.
- **No Condemnation:** The justified cannot be condemned (Rom. 8:1, 33–34).
- **Assurance:** Believers can have **full assurance** of their justification (Rom. 5:1–2; 1 John 5:13).

> *"God doth continue to forgive the sins of those that are justified; and although they can never fall from the state of justification, yet they may, by their sins, fall under God’s fatherly displeasure; and in that condition they usually do not have the light of His countenance restored unto them, until they humble themselves, confess their sins, beg pardon, and renew their faith and repentance."* (11.5)

**Key Distinction:**
- **Justification** (legal standing) is **permanent**.
- **Fellowship** with God can be disrupted by sin, requiring repentance (1 John 1:9).

---

### **6. Contrast with Roman Catholicism**
The 1689 Confession **explicitly rejects** Roman Catholic teachings on justification, such as:
- **Infused Righteousness:** Justification is **not** a process of making the sinner inherently righteous (contra Trent, Session 6).
- **Merit of Works:** Good works **do not** contribute to justification (contra Trent, Canon 32).
- **Faith + Works:** Justification is **by faith alone**, not faith **and** works (contra James 2:24 misinterpretation).
- **Sacramental Justification:** Justification is **not** mediated through baptism or other sacraments (contra Trent, Session 6).

---

### **7. Practical Implications**
- **Gospel Clarity:** Justification is **not** about what we do but what Christ has done.
- **Assurance:** Believers can be **certain** of their right standing before God.
- **Holiness:** While justification is by faith alone, it **produces** good works (Eph. 2:10).
- **Humility:** Justification **excludes boasting** (Rom. 3:27).

---

### **Key Scripture References in the Confession**
- **Romans 3:24–28** – Justification by grace through faith.
- **Romans 4:5–8** – Abraham justified by faith, not works.
- **Romans 5:18–19** – Christ’s obedience imputed to believers.
- **2 Corinthians 5:21** – Christ made sin for us, that we might be made righteous.
- **Galatians 2:16** – No justification by works of the law.
- **Philippians 3:9** – Righteousness through faith in Christ.

---

### **Conclusion**
The 1689 London Baptist Confession presents a **classic Protestant view of justification**, emphasizing:
1. **Sola Fide** (by faith alone),
2. **Sola Gratia** (by grace alone),
3. **Solus Christus** (in Christ alone),
4. **Sola Scriptura** (according to Scripture alone).

It rejects any form of **legalism, sacramentalism, or works-righteousness**, affirming that justification is a **free gift** received by faith in Christ’s finished work. This doctrine is foundational for **Reformed Baptist theology** and remains a key distinction from Roman Catholic and other non-Protestant views.

questions.response:
The **1689 London Baptist Confession of Faith** (also known as the **Second London Baptist Confession**) teaches a robust doctrine of the **perseverance of the saints** in **Chapter 17**, which aligns closely with the Reformed tradition. Here is a summary of its key teachings:

### **Chapter 17: Of the Perseverance of the Saints**
1. **The Certainty of Perseverance**
   - Those whom God has effectually called and regenerated, and who are united to Christ by faith, **cannot totally or finally fall away from the state of grace**.
   - They will **certainly persevere to the end** and be eternally saved (John 10:28–29; Phil. 1:6; 1 Pet. 1:5).

2. **The Means of Perseverance**
   - Believers persevere **not by their own strength**, but by the **grace and power of God** (1 Pet. 1:5).
   - God preserves them through **faith, prayer, the Word, the sacraments, and the ministry of the church** (Heb. 10:23–25; Jude 20–21).

3. **The Reality of Struggle and Sin**
   - While true believers **cannot lose their salvation**, they may **fall into grievous sins** and experience **spiritual weakness** (Ps. 51:12; Gal. 6:1).
   - However, God **chastens and restores** them (Heb. 12:6–7; 1 John 5:16–17).

4. **Assurance of Salvation**
   - Believers may have **full assurance** of their salvation, though this assurance can be shaken by sin, doubt, or trials (2 Pet. 1:10; 1 John 5:13).
   - True assurance comes from **faith in Christ, the testimony of the Spirit, and the fruit of obedience** (Rom. 8:16; Gal. 5:22–23).

5. **The Security of the Elect**
   - The perseverance of the saints is **grounded in God’s eternal decree, Christ’s intercession, and the Spirit’s sealing** (Rom. 8:30; Heb. 7:25; Eph. 1:13–14).
   - Even if a believer **temporarily falls into unbelief or sin**, God will **restore them** before death (Luke 22:32; 1 Cor. 11:32).

### **Key Differences from Other Views**
- **Contrast with Arminianism**: Unlike Arminian theology, which teaches that believers can **lose their salvation**, the 1689 Confession affirms that true believers **cannot finally fall away**.
- **Contrast with Antinomianism**: While salvation is secure, the Confession rejects the idea that believers can **live in unrepentant sin** without consequence (Rom. 6:1–2; Heb. 10:26–27).

### **Conclusion**
The 1689 London Baptist Confession teaches that **true believers are eternally secure in Christ**, not because of their own strength, but because of **God’s sovereign grace and faithfulness**. However, this security does not negate the need for **holiness, repentance, and dependence on God** in the Christian life.

The end of Gods appointing this Day, is for the manifestation of the glory of his Mercy, in the Eternal Salvation of the Elect; and of his Justice in the Eternal damnation of the Reprobate, who are wicked and disobedient; for then shall the Righteous go into Everlasting Life, and receive that fulness of Joy, and Glory, with everlasting reward, in the presence of the Lord: but the wicked who know not God, and obey not the Gospel of Jesus Christ, shall be cast into Eternal torments, and punished with everlasting destruction, from the presence of the Lord, and from the glory of his power. questions.response:
The **1689 London Baptist Confession of Faith** (also known as the **Second London Baptist Confession**) provides a clear and detailed Reformed Baptist perspective on the **last judgment**, aligning closely with historic Reformed theology while emphasizing Baptist distinctives. Here is a summary of its teaching on the subject, primarily drawn from **Chapter 32: Of the Last Judgment**:

---

### **1. The Certainty and Necessity of the Last Judgment**
- **God has appointed a day** in which He will judge the world in righteousness by Jesus Christ (Acts 17:31; Rom. 2:16).
- This judgment is **necessary** to vindicate God’s justice, display His glory, and fulfill His purposes in creation and redemption.
- The exact **time** of this day is unknown to men (Matt. 24:36), but it will come suddenly and unexpectedly (1 Thess. 5:2).

---

### **2. The Judge: Jesus Christ**
- The **Lord Jesus Christ**, who was unjustly judged by men, will be the **sole Judge** of all (John 5:22, 27; Acts 17:31).
- He will judge **all people**—both the living and the dead (2 Tim. 4:1; 1 Pet. 4:5).
- The Father has committed all judgment to the Son (John 5:22), who will execute it in perfect righteousness.

---

### **3. The Subjects of Judgment**
- **All people** who have ever lived will be judged:
  - The **righteous** (those united to Christ by faith) will be judged for their works to determine **rewards** (1 Cor. 3:12–15; 2 Cor. 5:10).
  - The **wicked** (those who rejected Christ) will be judged for their sins to determine **eternal punishment** (Matt. 25:46; Rev. 20:12–15).
- **Angels** who sinned will also be judged (2 Pet. 2:4; Jude 6).

---

### **4. The Nature of the Judgment**
- The judgment will be **public and universal**—every person’s deeds, words, and thoughts will be brought to light (Eccl. 12:14; Matt. 12:36; Rom. 2:16).
- The **books** (records of deeds) will be opened, and the **Book of Life** will be consulted (Rev. 20:12).
- The wicked will be **condemned** for their sins, especially their rejection of Christ (John 3:18, 36).
- The righteous will be **acquitted** on the basis of Christ’s imputed righteousness (Rom. 8:1, 33–34) and rewarded according to their works (Matt. 25:21, 23; 1 Cor. 3:8).

---

### **5. The Outcome of the Judgment**
- **For the wicked**:
  - Eternal **punishment in hell** (Matt. 25:41, 46; Rev. 14:11).
  - The punishment will be **just, conscious, and everlasting** (Matt. 25:46; Mark 9:48).
- **For the righteous**:
  - Eternal **life in the new heavens and new earth** (Matt. 25:46; Rev. 21:1–4).
  - Full **glorification**—freedom from sin, suffering, and death (1 Cor. 15:54–57; Rev. 21:4).
  - The **beatific vision**—seeing God face to face (1 John 3:2; Rev. 22:4).

---

### **6. The Final State After Judgment**
- The **new creation** will be established, where righteousness dwells (2 Pet. 3:13).
- The wicked will be **cast into the lake of fire** (Rev. 20:14–15).
- The righteous will **inherit the kingdom** prepared for them from the foundation of the world (Matt. 25:34).
- There will be **no more sin, death, or curse** (Rev. 21:4; 22:3).

---

### **Key Differences from Other Confessions**
While the **1689 Confession** closely follows the **Westminster Confession (1646)** and the **Savoy Declaration (1658)** on the last judgment, its Baptist distinctives are evident in:
1. **Believer’s Baptism** – The confession assumes that only **professing believers** (those baptized upon credible profession of faith) are part of the visible church, which affects the application of judgment (though all people, baptized or not, will be judged).
2. **Covenant Theology** – The 1689 Confession’s view of the covenants (especially the **New Covenant**) shapes its understanding of who is **righteous** (only those in Christ by faith) and who is **wicked** (those outside of Christ).

---

### **Scriptural Support in the Confession**
The confession cites numerous passages, including:
- **Matthew 25:31–46** (Sheep and Goats)
- **John 5:22–29** (Christ as Judge)
- **Acts 17:31** (God has appointed a day)
- **Romans 2:5–16** (Judgment according to works)
- **2 Corinthians 5:10** (Judgment seat of Christ)
- **Revelation 20:11–15** (Great White Throne Judgment)

---

### **Summary of Key Points**
| **Aspect**               | **Teaching of the 1689 Confession** |
|--------------------------|------------------------------------|
| **Judge**                | Jesus Christ (John 5:22) |
| **Subjects**             | All people (living & dead), angels (2 Tim. 4:1) |
| **Basis of Judgment**    | Works (for rewards/punishment), faith in Christ (for justification) |
| **Outcome for Wicked**   | Eternal punishment in hell (Matt. 25:46) |
| **Outcome for Righteous**| Eternal life in the new creation (Rev. 21:1–4) |
| **Purpose**              | Vindication of God’s justice, display of His glory |

---

### **Practical Implications**
1. **Urgency of the Gospel** – Since all will face judgment, the church must proclaim Christ (2 Cor. 5:11).
2. **Holiness of Life** – Believers should live in light of the coming judgment (1 John 3:3).
3. **Assurance for Believers** – Those in Christ need not fear condemnation (Rom. 8:1).
4. **Warning to the Unrepentant** – The wicked should flee to Christ for mercy (Heb. 2:3).

The **1689 Confession** presents a **sober yet hopeful** view of the last judgment—one that calls sinners to repentance while assuring believers of their eternal security in Christ.

questions.response:
The question of whether fallen man can choose God of his own free will is a central issue in Christian theology, particularly in the debate between **Calvinism** and **Arminianism**. Here’s a breakdown of the two main perspectives:

### **1. Calvinist Perspective (Reformed Theology)**
Calvinists (following John Calvin and the Synod of Dort) teach **total depravity**—that after the Fall, human nature is completely corrupted by sin, rendering man spiritually dead and unable to choose God on his own. Key points include:
- **Total Inability**: Fallen man cannot choose God because his will is enslaved to sin (Romans 3:10-12; Ephesians 2:1-3).
- **Monergism**: Salvation is entirely the work of God (John 6:44; Ephesians 2:8-9). Man does not cooperate in his regeneration; God alone regenerates the heart, enabling faith.
- **Irresistible Grace**: When God calls the elect, they *will* respond (John 6:37, 44).
- **Unconditional Election**: God chooses individuals for salvation based solely on His sovereign will, not human merit (Romans 9:16).

**Conclusion (Calvinist):** Fallen man cannot choose God of his own free will; God must first regenerate the heart to enable faith.

---

### **2. Arminian Perspective (Wesleyan/Classical Arminianism)**
Arminians (following Jacobus Arminius) teach **prevenient grace**—that God’s grace enables fallen man to respond to the Gospel, restoring a measure of free will. Key points include:
- **Prevenient Grace**: God’s grace precedes and enables human response (John 1:9; Titus 2:11). This grace is resistible but sufficient to allow a genuine choice.
- **Free Will**: While man is depraved, God’s grace restores the ability to choose or reject Him (John 3:16; Revelation 22:17).
- **Conditional Election**: God elects those He foreknows will respond in faith (Romans 8:29-30; 1 Peter 1:2).
- **Resistible Grace**: Man can reject God’s call (Matthew 23:37; Acts 7:51).

**Conclusion (Arminian):** Fallen man, enabled by prevenient grace, can choose God of his own free will.

---

### **3. Other Views**
- **Lutheranism**: Teaches **bondage of the will** (similar to Calvinism) but emphasizes that God’s Word and Spirit work through the Gospel to create faith (Romans 10:17).
- **Roman Catholicism**: Teaches that man, though wounded by sin, retains free will and can cooperate with grace (synergism).
- **Pelagianism** (heretical): Taught that man can choose God without grace, which was condemned at the Council of Ephesus (431 AD).

---

### **Key Biblical Passages**
- **Supporting Calvinism**:
  - *"No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him"* (John 6:44).
  - *"The mind governed by the flesh is hostile to God; it does not submit to God’s law, nor can it do so"* (Romans 8:7).
  - *"You did not choose me, but I chose you"* (John 15:16).

- **Supporting Arminianism**:
  - *"Whoever is thirsty, let him come; and whoever wishes, let him take the free gift of the water of life"* (Revelation 22:17).
  - *"God our Savior… wants all people to be saved and to come to a knowledge of the truth"* (1 Timothy 2:3-4).
  - *"Choose for yourselves this day whom you will serve"* (Joshua 24:15).

---

### **Final Thoughts**
The debate hinges on how one interprets **human depravity**, **God’s sovereignty**, and **the role of grace**. Calvinists emphasize God’s initiative, while Arminians emphasize human responsibility. Both agree that salvation is by grace alone, but they differ on how that grace operates in relation to free will.

questions.response:
The question of whether an unregenerate (unsaved) person can do anything *spiritually good* in God’s sight is a significant theological issue, particularly within Reformed theology. The answer depends on how one defines "spiritually good" and how one understands human nature after the Fall. Here’s a biblical and theological breakdown:

### **1. The Biblical Teaching on Human Depravity**
The Bible teaches that humanity is *totally depraved* (not that every person is as evil as possible, but that sin has corrupted every aspect of human nature—mind, will, emotions, and body). Key passages include:
- **Romans 3:10-12** – *"None is righteous, no, not one; no one understands; no one seeks for God. All have turned aside; together they have become worthless; no one does good, not even one."*
- **Ephesians 2:1-3** – *"And you were dead in the trespasses and sins in which you once walked... and were by nature children of wrath, like the rest of mankind."*
- **Jeremiah 17:9** – *"The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick; who can understand it?"*
- **John 6:44** – *"No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him."*

These passages indicate that, apart from God’s grace, humans are spiritually dead, unable to please God, and incapable of true spiritual good.

### **2. What Does "Spiritually Good" Mean?**
In theology, "spiritually good" (or *meritorious* before God) refers to actions that:
- **Proceed from a heart regenerated by the Holy Spirit** (John 3:3-8).
- **Are done out of love for God and neighbor** (Matthew 22:37-39; 1 Corinthians 13:3).
- **Are done in faith** (Hebrews 11:6; Romans 14:23).
- **Are done for God’s glory** (1 Corinthians 10:31).

An unregenerate person, by definition, lacks saving faith, a regenerate heart, and the indwelling Holy Spirit. Therefore, their actions—even if outwardly moral—are not *spiritually good* in God’s sight because they are not done for His glory or out of love for Him.

### **3. Can the Unregenerate Do *Outwardly* Good Deeds?**
Yes, unregenerate people can perform *outwardly* good deeds (e.g., charity, kindness, honesty) because:
- **Common Grace** – God restrains evil and enables all people to do relative good in society (Matthew 5:45; Acts 14:17).
- **Natural Law** – Even fallen humans retain a sense of right and wrong (Romans 2:14-15).
- **Civic Righteousness** – Many unbelievers live morally upright lives (e.g., non-Christian parents loving their children, honest businesspeople).

However, these deeds are **not spiritually good** in God’s sight because:
- They are **not done in faith** (Hebrews 11:6).
- They are **not done for God’s glory** (1 Corinthians 10:31).
- They are **tainted by sinful motives** (Isaiah 64:6; Philippians 3:7-9).

### **4. Theological Perspectives**
Different Christian traditions have nuanced views on this:

#### **A. Reformed Theology (Calvinism)**
- **Total Depravity** – Unregenerate people cannot do anything truly good in God’s sight because their nature is corrupt.
- **Works Righteousness** – Even "good" deeds are filthy rags before God (Isaiah 64:6).
- **Common Grace** – God enables unbelievers to do relative good in society, but it is not saving or meritorious.

#### **B. Arminian/Wesleyan Theology**
- **Prevenient Grace** – God’s grace enables all people to respond to the Gospel, and some good works may be done in cooperation with this grace.
- **Partial Depravity** – Humans are corrupted but not utterly incapable of responding to God’s grace.

#### **C. Roman Catholic Theology**
- **Natural Good** – Unbelievers can perform naturally good acts (e.g., charity, justice) that are pleasing to God, though not meritorious for salvation.
- **Supernatural Good** – Only the regenerate (baptized) can perform truly meritorious works through grace.

#### **D. Lutheran Theology**
- **Simul Justus et Peccator** – Even believers remain sinners, but their good works are acceptable to God *because of Christ’s righteousness*, not their own merit.
- **Unbelievers’ Works** – Their works are not truly good because they lack faith.

### **5. Key Biblical Distinctions**
- **Outward Good vs. Spiritual Good** – An unbeliever may feed the poor (outward good), but if not done in faith, it is not spiritually good (1 Corinthians 13:3).
- **Legal Righteousness vs. Gospel Righteousness** – The Pharisees had legal righteousness (Matthew 23:23) but lacked love for God (Matthew 15:8).
- **Works of the Law vs. Works of Faith** – Paul contrasts works done to earn salvation (Romans 3:20) with works done in faith (James 2:17-26).

### **6. Practical Implications**
- **Salvation is by Grace Alone** – No one can earn God’s favor through good works (Ephesians 2:8-9).
- **Good Works Flow from Regeneration** – True good works are the *fruit* of salvation, not the *cause* (Ephesians 2:10; Titus 2:14).
- **Judgment is Based on Christ’s Righteousness** – Believers are accepted not because of their works but because of Christ’s (2 Corinthians 5:21).

### **Conclusion**
An unregenerate person **cannot** do anything *spiritually good* in God’s sight because:
1. Their nature is corrupted by sin (Romans 3:10-12).
2. Their works are not done in faith (Hebrews 11:6).
3. Their motives are not pure (Isaiah 64:6).
4. They lack the Holy Spirit (Romans 8:7-8).

However, God in His **common grace** allows unbelievers to do *outwardly* good deeds that benefit society, but these are not *spiritually* good in His sight. Only the regenerate, who have been made new in Christ (2 Corinthians 5:17), can perform works that are truly pleasing to God.

questions.response:
The question of whether *the Fall* (the biblical account of humanity's disobedience in Genesis 3) affects *every part of human nature* is a central and deeply debated topic in Christian theology, particularly in discussions about **original sin**, **human anthropology**, and **salvation**. The answer depends on how one defines "human nature" and interprets the consequences of the Fall. Below are key perspectives from different theological traditions:

---

### **1. The Augustinian/Reformed View (Total Depravity)**
**Position:** The Fall affects *every aspect* of human nature—intellect, will, emotions, desires, and even the body—rendering humanity spiritually dead, morally corrupt, and incapable of true good apart from God's grace.

- **Key Points:**
  - **Total Depravity (not "utter depravity"):** Every faculty of human nature is tainted by sin, though not always to the same degree. Humans are not as evil as they *could* be, but sin has corrupted every part of them.
  - **Intellect:** The mind is darkened (Eph. 4:18; Rom. 1:21), leading to futile thinking and idolatry.
  - **Will:** The will is enslaved to sin (John 8:34; Rom. 6:16-20) and cannot choose God without grace (John 6:44).
  - **Emotions/Desires:** Affections are disordered (Jer. 17:9; Rom. 1:24-25), leading to self-love over love for God.
  - **Body:** Physical death and decay are consequences of sin (Gen. 3:19; Rom. 5:12).
  - **Imputation of Sin:** Adam's guilt is imputed to all humanity (Rom. 5:12-21), making all "by nature children of wrath" (Eph. 2:3).

- **Scriptural Support:**
  - Romans 3:10-18 ("None is righteous, no, not one...")
  - Psalm 51:5 ("Behold, I was brought forth in iniquity...")
  - Ephesians 2:1-3 ("dead in trespasses and sins...")

- **Theological Implications:**
  - Salvation is entirely by God's grace (monergism).
  - Humanity cannot contribute to its own redemption.
  - Even "good" works are tainted by sin (Isa. 64:6).

---

### **2. The Eastern Orthodox View (Ancestral Sin)**
**Position:** The Fall introduced *death and corruption* into human nature, but human nature itself was not *totally* corrupted. The image of God (imago Dei) remains, though the *likeness* (moral conformity to God) was lost.

- **Key Points:**
  - **No Imputed Guilt:** Adam's sin is not imputed to humanity; instead, we inherit *death* and *corruption* (Rom. 5:12: "death spread to all men because all sinned").
  - **Human Nature is Wounded, Not Totally Corrupt:** The intellect, will, and emotions are weakened but not entirely depraved. Humans retain the capacity to seek God (though imperfectly).
  - **Synergy (Cooperation with Grace):** Salvation involves human participation (theosis), though grace is primary.
  - **Physical Death as the Primary Consequence:** The Fall introduced mortality, which distorts human nature but does not destroy the image of God.

- **Scriptural Support:**
  - Genesis 1:26-27 (humans made in God's image).
  - Romans 2:14-15 (Gentiles "show the work of the law written on their hearts").
  - 1 Corinthians 15:22 ("in Adam all die...").

- **Theological Implications:**
  - Humans are not "totally depraved" but are "sick" and in need of healing.
  - Free will is not destroyed but is weakened (ancestral sin).
  - Salvation is a process of restoration (theosis), not just legal justification.

---

### **3. The Roman Catholic View (Original Sin and Concupiscence)**
**Position:** The Fall wounded human nature but did not totally corrupt it. Original sin is the *loss of original holiness and justice*, but the image of God remains, and human nature retains its essential goodness.

- **Key Points:**
  - **Original Sin as a "Stain":** Humans inherit a *privation* of grace (not guilt, in the Augustinian sense) and are born with concupiscence (inclination to sin).
  - **Human Nature is Wounded, Not Depraved:** The intellect is darkened, the will is weakened, and the passions are disordered, but humans can still do *natural good* (e.g., love, justice, truth).
  - **Prevenient Grace:** God's grace enables humans to cooperate with salvation (synergism).
  - **Baptism Removes Original Sin:** Infants are cleansed of original sin in baptism, though concupiscence remains.

- **Scriptural Support:**
  - Romans 2:14-15 (Gentiles do by nature what the law requires).
  - James 1:14-15 (sin arises from desire, not from human nature itself).
  - Council of Trent (1546): Original sin is "transmitted by propagation, not by imitation."

- **Theological Implications:**
  - Humans can perform *natural virtues* (e.g., kindness, courage) but cannot attain *supernatural* holiness without grace.
  - Salvation is a cooperative process (grace + free will).
  - The Fall introduced *disorder* but not total corruption.

---

### **4. The Pelagian/Semi-Pelagian View (Minimal Fallen Effects)**
**Position:** The Fall had little to no effect on human nature. Humans retain full moral freedom and can choose good or evil without divine assistance.

- **Key Points:**
  - **No Original Sin:** Adam's sin only set a bad example; humans are born morally neutral.
  - **Free Will is Unaffected:** Humans can choose God without grace (Pelagianism) or with minimal grace (Semi-Pelagianism).
  - **Rejected by Mainstream Christianity:** Both views were condemned at the Councils of Carthage (418) and Orange (529).

- **Scriptural Support (for Semi-Pelagianism):**
  - 1 Timothy 2:4 ("God desires all people to be saved...").
  - Revelation 3:20 ("Behold, I stand at the door and knock...").

- **Theological Implications:**
  - Salvation is largely a human effort (works-based).
  - Grace is helpful but not necessary for initial faith.

---

### **5. The Lutheran View (Simul Justus et Peccator)**
**Position:** The Fall totally corrupted human nature, but through faith, believers are *simultaneously* justified (declared righteous) and sinful.

- **Key Points:**
  - **Total Corruption:** Like the Reformed view, Lutherans affirm that sin affects every part of human nature.
  - **Simul Justus et Peccator:** "At the same time righteous and a sinner." Believers are declared righteous by faith but remain sinners in practice.
  - **Bondage of the Will:** Humans cannot choose God without grace (Luther's *Bondage of the Will*).
  - **Civil Righteousness:** Unbelievers can do *outwardly* good works (e.g., charity, justice) but not *spiritually* good works (those done out of love for God).

- **Scriptural Support:**
  - Romans 7:15-20 ("I do not do what I want, but I do the very thing I hate...").
  - Philippians 3:9 ("not having a righteousness of my own...").

- **Theological Implications:**
  - Salvation is entirely by grace through faith (sola fide).
  - Good works flow from faith but do not contribute to justification.

---

### **Summary of Views on the Fall's Effect on Human Nature**
| **Tradition**       | **Effect of the Fall**                          | **Human Nature After the Fall**               | **Salvation**                     |
|---------------------|-----------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------|
| **Reformed**        | Total depravity (every part corrupted)        | Spiritually dead, enslaved to sin             | Monergistic (God alone saves)     |
| **Eastern Orthodox**| Death and corruption (nature wounded)         | Image of God intact, but likeness lost        | Synergistic (grace + human effort)|
| **Roman Catholic**  | Wounded nature (concupiscence)                | Image of God remains, but disordered          | Synergistic (grace + free will)   |
| **Lutheran**        | Total corruption (but simul justus et peccator)| Spiritually dead, but declared righteous      | Monergistic (grace alone)         |
| **Pelagian**        | No effect (only bad example)                  | Morally neutral, free to choose good          | Works-based                       |

questions.response:
The question of whether God saves people based on *foreseen faith* (the idea that God elects individuals to salvation because He foresees their future faith) is a significant theological debate, particularly between **Calvinist** and **Arminian** perspectives. Here’s a breakdown of the key views:

### **1. Arminian/Wesleyan View: God Saves Based on Foreseen Faith**
- **Key Idea:** God elects people to salvation because He foresees (knows in advance) that they will freely choose to believe in Christ.
- **Biblical Support:**
  - **Romans 8:29-30** – "For those whom He foreknew, He also predestined..." (Arminians argue that "foreknew" means God knew who would believe).
  - **1 Peter 1:1-2** – "Elect according to the foreknowledge of God..."
  - **John 3:16** – "Whoever believes in Him shall not perish..." (emphasis on human response).
- **Theological Basis:**
  - God’s election is **conditional**—based on human faith, which He foresees.
  - Human free will is preserved; God does not override it.
  - Salvation is available to all, but only those who believe are saved.

### **2. Calvinist View: God Saves Unconditionally (Not Based on Foreseen Faith)**
- **Key Idea:** God elects people to salvation **not** because of anything He foresees in them (including faith), but purely by His sovereign choice.
- **Biblical Support:**
  - **Ephesians 1:4-5** – "He chose us in Him before the foundation of the world... according to the good pleasure of His will."
  - **Romans 9:11-16** – "So then it depends not on human will or exertion, but on God, who has mercy."
  - **John 6:44** – "No one can come to Me unless the Father who sent Me draws him."
- **Theological Basis:**
  - God’s election is **unconditional**—not based on human merit, faith, or foreseen response.
  - Faith itself is a **gift from God** (Ephesians 2:8-9), not something humans generate on their own.
  - Human free will is real but **not autonomous**—it operates within God’s sovereign plan.

### **3. Other Perspectives**
- **Molinism (Middle Knowledge):** Some (like Luis de Molina) argue that God uses His **middle knowledge** (knowledge of what free creatures *would* do in any circumstance) to elect those He knows would freely choose Him.
- **Lutheran View:** Similar to Calvinism in emphasizing God’s sovereignty but with a stronger emphasis on **universal atonement** (Christ died for all, but only believers are saved).

### **Key Differences**
| **Issue**               | **Arminian View**                          | **Calvinist View**                          |
|-------------------------|-------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------|
| **Basis of Election**   | God foresees faith                       | God’s sovereign choice (unconditional)     |
| **Human Free Will**     | Free to accept or reject Christ          | Free, but only within God’s decree         |
| **Faith as a Gift?**    | No (human response)                      | Yes (Ephesians 2:8-9)                      |
| **Romans 9:16**         | "Depends on man’s will" (human choice)   | "Depends on God’s mercy" (sovereign grace) |

### **Conclusion**
- **If you believe God saves based on foreseen faith**, you likely hold an **Arminian or Wesleyan** view.
- **If you believe God saves unconditionally**, you likely hold a **Calvinist** view.
- **If you believe God uses middle knowledge to elect**, you may lean toward **Molinism**.

Both views seek to uphold **God’s sovereignty** and **human responsibility**, but they differ on how these two truths interact. Would you like to explore specific biblical passages in more depth?

questions.response:
The question of whether God's election of individuals to salvation is **conditional** or **unconditional** is a central debate in Christian theology, particularly between **Calvinist** and **Arminian** perspectives. Here’s a breakdown of the two views:

### **1. Unconditional Election (Calvinist View)**
- **Definition:** God chooses individuals for salvation based solely on His sovereign will, not on any foreseen merit, faith, or response in the person.
- **Key Scriptures:**
  - **Ephesians 1:4-5** – *"He chose us in him before the foundation of the world... In love he predestined us for adoption to himself."*
  - **Romans 9:11-16** – *"Though they were not yet born and had done nothing either good or bad... 'Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.'... So then it depends not on human will or exertion, but on God, who has mercy."*
  - **John 6:44** – *"No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him."*
- **Theological Basis:**
  - God’s election is **not based on human works or faith** (Romans 9:16).
  - Salvation is **entirely a work of God’s grace** (Ephesians 2:8-9).
  - Human depravity means **no one seeks God** (Romans 3:10-12), so election must be unconditional.
- **Implications:**
  - God’s choice is **sovereign and free**, not dependent on human response.
  - Election is **not unfair** because all deserve condemnation (Romans 3:23; 6:23).
  - Assurance of salvation is **firm** because it depends on God’s decree, not human effort.

### **2. Conditional Election (Arminian View)**
- **Definition:** God elects individuals based on His **foreknowledge** of who would freely respond to the Gospel in faith.
- **Key Scriptures:**
  - **1 Peter 1:1-2** – *"To those... chosen according to the foreknowledge of God."*
  - **Romans 8:29** – *"For those whom he foreknew he also predestined."*
  - **John 3:16** – *"Whoever believes in him shall not perish."*
  - **2 Peter 3:9** – *"The Lord... is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance."*
- **Theological Basis:**
  - God’s election is **based on His foreknowledge** of who would believe (Romans 8:29).
  - Human **free will** is real, and God respects it (Deuteronomy 30:19; Joshua 24:15).
  - God **desires all to be saved** (1 Timothy 2:4), so election must be conditional on faith.
- **Implications:**
  - Salvation is **available to all** but **effective only for those who believe**.
  - Human **responsibility** is emphasized—people must respond to the Gospel.
  - Assurance of salvation is **conditional** on persevering in faith.

### **Other Views (Middle Positions)**
Some theologians seek a **middle ground** between Calvinism and Arminianism:
- **Molinism (Luis de Molina):** God uses **middle knowledge** (knowledge of what free creatures would do in any circumstance) to elect those He knows would respond to grace.
- **Amyraldianism (4-Point Calvinism):** God **universally desires salvation** (like Arminianism) but **effectually calls the elect** (like Calvinism).
- **Wesleyan-Arminianism:** Emphasizes **prevenient grace** (grace that enables all to respond to the Gospel), making election conditional on faith but still gracious.

### **Key Differences Summarized**
| **Issue**               | **Unconditional Election (Calvinism)** | **Conditional Election (Arminianism)** |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------|----------------------------------------|
| **Basis of Election**   | God’s sovereign will alone             | God’s foreknowledge of faith           |
| **Human Free Will**     | Compatibilist (free will within God’s decree) | Libertarian (genuine free choice) |
| **God’s Desire**        | Some are elected, others are not       | God desires all to be saved            |
| **Assurance of Salvation** | Strong (based on God’s decree)      | Conditional (based on perseverance)    |
| **Key Passages**        | Romans 9, Ephesians 1, John 6          | 1 Peter 1, Romans 8:29, 2 Peter 3:9    |

### **Conclusion**
- **Calvinists** argue that **unconditional election** best preserves God’s sovereignty and grace.
- **Arminians** argue that **conditional election** best preserves human responsibility and God’s universal love.
- **Scripture contains elements of both**, leading to ongoing debate.

Would you like a deeper exploration of any particular aspect (e.g., historical development, objections to each view, or how this affects evangelism)?

questions.response:
The question of whether God chose His elect before the foundation of the world is a central topic in **Reformed theology** (Calvinism) and is rooted in several key biblical passages. Here’s a biblical and theological exploration of the issue:

### **1. Biblical Support for Election Before the Foundation of the World**
Several Scriptures explicitly state that God’s choice of the elect was made **before creation**:

- **Ephesians 1:4-5 (ESV)**
  > *"Even as he chose us in him **before the foundation of the world**, that we should be holy and blameless before him. In love he predestined us for adoption to himself as sons through Jesus Christ, according to the purpose of his will..."*
  - This passage clearly teaches that God’s election of believers was **not based on foreseen faith** but was an **eternal decree** made before time began.

- **2 Timothy 1:9 (ESV)**
  > *"[God] who saved us and called us to a holy calling, not because of our works but because of his own purpose and grace, **which he gave us in Christ Jesus before the ages began**..."*
  - Salvation is rooted in God’s **eternal purpose**, not human merit.

- **Revelation 13:8 (KJV)**
  > *"...the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world."*
  - The atonement was planned **before creation**, implying that those for whom Christ died were also chosen beforehand.

- **Romans 8:29-30 (ESV)**
  > *"For those whom he **foreknew** he also **predestined** to be conformed to the image of his Son... And those whom he predestined he also called, and those whom he called he also justified, and those whom he justified he also glorified."*
  - The term **"foreknew"** (Greek: *proginōskō*) in this context does not mean mere foreknowledge of future actions but **God’s sovereign choice** (cf. Romans 11:2, where "foreknew" refers to God’s election of Israel).

- **Acts 13:48 (ESV)**
  > *"And when the Gentiles heard this, they began rejoicing and glorifying the word of the Lord, and as many as were **appointed to eternal life** believed."*
  - Faith is the result of God’s **appointment**, not the cause of it.

### **2. Theological Perspectives on Election**
Different Christian traditions interpret these passages in varying ways:

#### **A. Calvinism (Reformed Theology)**
- **Unconditional Election**: God chooses individuals for salvation **not based on foreseen faith or merit** but solely according to His sovereign will (Eph. 1:4-5; Rom. 9:11-16).
- **Double Predestination**: Some Calvinists (e.g., John Calvin, the Canons of Dort) teach that God actively elects some to salvation and **passively permits** others to remain in their sin (though this is debated even among Calvinists).
- **Irresistible Grace**: The elect **cannot ultimately resist** God’s call (John 6:37, 44).

#### **B. Arminianism (Wesleyan/Methodist)**
- **Conditional Election**: God elects those whom He **foreknows will believe** (Rom. 8:29 interpreted as foreknowledge of faith).
- **Corporate Election**: Some Arminians argue that God elects **a people (the Church)** rather than individuals, and individuals enter that election by faith.
- **Resistible Grace**: Humans can **reject** God’s call (Matt. 23:37; Heb. 6:4-6).

#### **C. Molinism (Middle Knowledge)**
- Proposed by Luis de Molina, this view suggests that God **knows all possible free choices** and elects based on what He knows humans would freely choose.
- This attempts to reconcile **divine sovereignty** with **human free will**.

#### **D. Lutheranism**
- Similar to Calvinism in affirming **monergism** (God alone saves), but differs on **double predestination** (Lutherans generally reject it).
- Election is **in Christ** (Eph. 1:4), not based on human merit.

### **3. Key Objections & Responses**
#### **Objection 1: "Doesn’t this make God unfair?"**
- **Response**: God is **sovereign** and has the right to show mercy to whom He wills (Rom. 9:14-18; Ex. 33:19).
- **Fairness** would mean everyone gets what they deserve (eternal punishment), but **grace** means some receive what they don’t deserve (salvation).

#### **Objection 2: "Doesn’t this make evangelism unnecessary?"**
- **Response**: God **ordains the means as well as the end** (Rom. 10:14-15). Election does not negate the **Great Commission**—it guarantees its success (Matt. 28:19-20; Acts 18:9-10).

#### **Objection 3: "Doesn’t this make God the author of sin?"**
- **Response**: God **permits** sin but does not **cause** it (James 1:13-15). He uses evil for His purposes (Gen. 50:20; Acts 2:23) without being morally culpable.

### **4. Practical Implications of Election**
- **Assurance of Salvation**: If God chose us before time, our salvation is **secure** (Rom. 8:30; Phil. 1:6).
- **Humility**: We contribute **nothing** to our salvation (Eph. 2:8-9; 1 Cor. 1:26-31).
- **Worship**: Election leads to **praise** for God’s grace (Eph. 1:6, 12, 14).
- **Evangelism**: We preach the Gospel **knowing God will save His elect** (2 Tim. 2:10).

### **5. Conclusion: Yes, God Chose His Elect Before the Foundation of the World**
The **clearest biblical teaching** (Eph. 1:4-5; 2 Tim. 1:9; Rom. 8:29-30) is that God’s election is:
- **Eternal** (before creation)
- **Unconditional** (not based on human merit)
- **Sovereign** (based on God’s will alone)
- **Effectual** (guarantees salvation)

This does not mean God is **arbitrary**—He elects **in Christ** (Eph. 1:4) and for His **glory** (Eph. 1:6, 12, 14). The mystery of election should lead us to **humility, worship, and evangelistic zeal**, trusting that God’s purposes will stand (Isa. 46:10).
